ocar.opportunity: High-resolution electron microscopy now yields volumes that can, in principle, support reconstruction of complex neural wiring.
ocar.challenge: Those volumes are so large and densely packed that segmenting and viewing neural processes is slow, difficult, and often done with purely manual tools.
ocar.action: Jeong, Beyer, Hadwiger, and colleagues present NeuroTrace: semi-automatic multiphase level-set segmentation with 3D tracking, plus GPU volume rendering that filters on demand, scores local histogram edges, and ray-casts implicit surfaces of segmented structures.
ocar.resolution: The system is designed to scale to large datasets and data-parallel hardware. Compared with a commonly used manual EM segmentation tool, the interactive NeuroTrace workflow is faster and easier for reconstructing complex neural processes.
ocar.future_work: The paper does not report numeric speedups or tests on a named public volume; a next step is measuring accuracy and throughput as volumes grow beyond the comparison shown here.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can now take extremely detailed pictures of nerve tissue, but the pictures are so big that tracing each nerve by hand takes too long. This paper describes a computer system that helps people outline nerves on screen more quickly and see them in three dimensions.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2009), Jeong, Beyer, Hadwiger, Pfister, Whitaker and colleagues introduce NeuroTrace for electron-microscopy volumes. Semi-automatic multiphase level-set segmentation with 3D tracking reconstructs neural processes, while specialized volume rendering uses view-dependent filtering, a local histogram edge metric, and on-the-fly interpolation and ray-casting of implicit surfaces. Both pieces run on the GPU for interactive performance and are meant to scale to large, data-parallel hardware. A comparison with a common manual EM segmentation tool finds the interactive workflow faster and easier for complex reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: The comparison is a workflow claim rather than a large benchmark suite: the abstract reports that NeuroTrace is faster and easier than a commonly used manual tool, without numeric speedups or error rates. Scalability is a design goal (GPU, on-demand filtering) rather than a demonstrated limit on particular volume sizes. The method is semi-automatic, so expert interaction remains in the loop.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can now take extremely detailed pictures of nerve tissue, but the pictures are so big that tracing each nerve by hand takes too long. This paper describes a computer system that helps people outline nerves on screen more quickly and see them in three dimensions.

ocar.opportunity: A complete connectional map is essential for relating neural structure to function, yet such maps had been obtained only in C. elegans.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian circuits are far larger, and even a single muscle’s motor innervation had not been reconstructed as a full connectome.
ocar.action: Lu, Tapia, White, and Lichtman reconstructed the connectomes of six interscutularis muscles from adult transgenic mice whose motor axons all expressed fluorescent proteins.
ocar.resolution: The maps supply an anatomical basis for graded tensions in the size principle; a quantitative relationship among axonal caliber, length, and synapse number; left–right structural variation unlike invertebrate stereotypy; and axonal wiring often longer than a length-minimizing design would predict. Mammalian muscle function is implemented with varied wiring diagrams that share global features but differ in form, possibly because synaptic competition dominates circuit assembly.
ocar.future_work: The authors present this as an attempt at mammalian circuits, not a general method for central brains; whether synaptic competition causes the observed variability is offered as a hypothesis, not a direct test.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring map of every nerve-to-muscle contact had previously been finished only in a tiny worm. This team mapped the motor nerves of six small mouse muscles and found that left and right sides, and even similar muscles, are wired quite differently.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2009), Lu, Tapia, White, and Lichtman reconstruct connectomes of six interscutularis muscles in adult transgenic mice with fluorescently labeled motor axons. The reconstructions support the size principle’s anatomical basis, a robust link among axonal caliber, length, and synapse number, and substantial left–right structural variation in identified neurons, in contrast to invertebrate stereotypy. Axons are often longer than a wiring-length minimum would require. The authors conclude that mammalian muscle function uses varied diagrams that share global features, with variability possibly arising from synaptic competition.
summaries.advanced: The dataset is six muscles in one peripheral circuit, not a central mammalian connectome. Competition as the source of variability is presented as a possible explanation, not a causal experiment. Wiring-length claims are relative to a widely held minimization view rather than a fitted null model reported in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring map of every nerve-to-muscle contact had previously been finished only in a tiny worm. This team mapped the motor nerves of six small mouse muscles and found that left and right sides, and even similar muscles, are wired quite differently.

ocar.opportunity: A common claim in neuroscience is that genetic properties of neurons strongly shape their synaptic networks, but that idea had rarely been tested at nervous-system scale.
ocar.challenge: Doing so requires matched connectivity and gene-expression signatures for many identified neurons, which few animals provide.
ocar.action: Kaufman, Dror, Meilijson, and Ruppin use the C. elegans wiring diagram plus cellular gene-expression data and two complementary assays to ask whether a neuron’s expression signature carries information about its connectivity signature.
ocar.resolution: Expression signatures carry significant information about synaptic connectivity, and the authors identify a list of putative genes that predict neural connectivity. The relation is especially marked in subsets of neurons.
ocar.future_work: They present the gene list as a starting point for more detailed computational and experimental follow-up, not as a finished causal map of how genes specify synapses.

summaries.beginner: People often assume that a nerve cell’s genes help decide whom it connects to, but that is hard to test in a whole nervous system. Using the worm C. elegans, this study shows that a cell’s gene activity does carry clues about its wiring, and it points to genes that may help predict connections.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2006), Kaufman, Dror, Meilijson, and Ruppin quantify the link between gene-expression and synaptic-connectivity signatures in C. elegans, whose wiring diagram and cellular expression data cover most neurons. Two complementary assays show that expression carries significant information about connectivity and yield a list of putative predictive genes. The relationship is highly marked in identified neuronal subsets. The results are framed as a starting point for further computational and experimental work.
summaries.advanced: The abstract reports that expression “carries significant information” and identifies putative genes; it does not claim that those genes causally build synapses, nor does it give an effect size beyond “significant.” Coverage is “most” neurons, not a complete paired matrix. Predictive genes remain candidates pending follow-up.

plain_language_summary: People often assume that a nerve cell’s genes help decide whom it connects to, but that is hard to test in a whole nervous system. Using the worm C. elegans, this study shows that a cell’s gene activity does carry clues about its wiring, and it points to genes that may help predict connections.

ocar.opportunity: Physiology of CA3→CA1 synapses shows both pre- and postsynaptic effects, so axonal boutons might act as local compartments for efficacy and microconnectivity.
ocar.challenge: Testing that idea requires three-dimensional morphology and composition of a relatively homogeneous axon population, not just 2D snapshots.
ocar.action: Shepherd and Harris used serial electron microscopy in hippocampal slices to map postsynaptic densities, vesicles, and mitochondria along 75 CA3→CA1 axon segments in mid-stratum radiatum of CA1, fully reconstructing eleven axons.
ocar.resolution: Synapses occurred on average every 2.7 μm. Most varicosities (68%) had one PSD, 19% had 2–4, and 13% had none; 90% contained vesicles, 53% lacked mitochondria, and 8% contained only mitochondria. Varicosities varied greatly in length and volume, while intervaricosity shafts were narrow (0.17 ± 0.04 μm) and spine-neck-like, suggesting biochemical compartmentalization and localized differences in metabolism and connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The findings raise, rather than resolve, how boutons without mitochondria regulate ATP and Ca2+, and whether localized metabolic and connectivity differences are used in plasticity.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells talk at tiny swellings along their outgoing fibers, but it was unclear how separate those swellings really are. By stacking electron-microscope pictures of rat hippocampus, this study shows that the swellings differ a lot in size and contents, and that the thin segments between them could keep each swelling’s chemistry somewhat private.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Neuroscience (1998), Shepherd and Harris reconstruct CA3→CA1 axons in hippocampal slices with serial electron microscopy. Along 75 segments (9.1 ± 2.0 μm), synapses defined by colocalized PSDs and vesicles occurred on average every 2.7 μm. Most varicosities (68%) had one PSD, 19% had two to four, and 13% had none; vesicles were in 90% of varicosities, mitochondria were absent from 53%, and 8% held only mitochondria. Eleven fully reconstructed axons showed oblong, highly variable varicosities and narrow tubular shafts (0.17 ± 0.04 μm), which the authors analogize to spine necks as possible biochemical compartments.
summaries.advanced: The sample is a nearly homogeneous CA3→CA1 population in the middle of stratum radiatum of slices, not in vivo whole axons. Mitochondrial absence “raises questions” about ATP and Ca2+ regulation rather than measuring those quantities. Compartmentalization and localized metabolic differences are morphological inferences. Organism is rat hippocampus (catalog organism tag: other).

plain_language_summary: Brain cells talk at tiny swellings along their outgoing fibers, but it was unclear how separate those swellings really are. By stacking electron-microscope pictures of rat hippocampus, this study shows that the swellings differ a lot in size and contents, and that the thin segments between them could keep each swelling’s chemistry somewhat private.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy datasets keep growing in size and resolution, making high-performance computing a practical necessity for processing and analysis.
ocar.challenge: HPC systems are powerful but not, by default, easy for a microscopy community to use for private and shared data, alignment, segmentation, and simulation.
ocar.action: Carson, Brown, Labyer, Harris, and colleagues adapt TACC’s Core Experience Portal into 3dem.org, a browser-based science gateway linked to TACC HPC and optionally to other storage and compute systems.
ocar.resolution: The gateway gives the 3DEM community access to raw and processed datasets (private and shared), image-processing tools for alignment and segmentation, and simulation and analysis environments, bridging advanced EM with scalable HPC.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the portal as infrastructure for discovery rather than a completed scientific result; connecting additional compute sites and showing uptake on community volumes remain implicit next steps.

summaries.beginner: Three-dimensional electron-microscope pictures of tissue are now so large that ordinary computers cannot keep up. This paper describes a website that lets researchers send that work to a supercomputing center through a browser.
summaries.intermediate: In SN Computer Science (2026), Carson, Harris, Sejnowski and colleagues describe 3dem.org, a customization of the Texas Advanced Computing Center Core Experience Portal for volumetric electron microscopy. The science gateway offers browser access to private and shared raw and processed datasets, alignment and segmentation tools, and simulation and analysis environments, all linked to TACC HPC with the option to attach other storage and compute systems. The stated goal is scalable, accessible infrastructure that bridges 3DEM with HPC.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods/infrastructure paper: no benchmark timings, dataset sizes, or user-study metrics appear in the abstract. Claims about bridging EM and HPC describe the designed capability of the gateway, not a quantified throughput result. Utility will depend on how the community actually uses 3dem.org and which external systems get connected.

plain_language_summary: Three-dimensional electron-microscope pictures of tissue are now so large that ordinary computers cannot keep up. This paper describes a website that lets researchers send that work to a supercomputing center through a browser.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans shares conserved genetic pathways with humans, has a fully mapped connectome, and shows progressive structural and functional decline with age, making it a compact model of neuronal aging and degeneration.
ocar.challenge: The literature on worm neural communication, disease modeling, and translational assays is spread across genetics, behavior, pharmacology, and genomics.
ocar.action: Pan, Shen, Peng, and colleagues review the worm’s advantages—quantifiable behavior, short lifespan, genetic tractability—its neural communication architecture, and its use in molecular models of neurodegenerative disease.
ocar.resolution: They also cover high-throughput pharmacological screening, environmental toxicology, and advanced genomic sequencing, aiming at a framework for neurodegenerative mechanisms and clinical translation under stress conditions, particularly hypoxia.
ocar.future_work: As a review, the paper synthesizes rather than reports new experiments; applying that framework under hypoxia and other stresses to clinical translation is the agenda it sets.

summaries.beginner: The tiny worm C. elegans has a simple, fully mapped nervous system and genes that resemble many human genes. This review explains why that worm is useful for studying how nerve cells age and how brain diseases might start.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience (2026), Pan, Shen, Peng, Liu and colleagues review C. elegans as a model of neuronal aging and degeneration. They emphasize conserved pathways with extensive human-gene homology, a streamlined fully mapped connectome, quantifiable behavior, short lifespan, and genetic tractability. The review covers neural communication architecture, molecular models of neurodegenerative disease, and integration with pharmacological screening, environmental toxicology, and genomic sequencing, with an eye toward translation under stress, particularly hypoxia.
summaries.advanced: This is a synthesis, not a new connectome or intervention trial. Clinical-translation language in the abstract is aspirational and specifically tied to stress conditions such as hypoxia. Catalog stages include infrastructure; the scientific content is a review of a model organism rather than a new data resource.

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm C. elegans has a simple, fully mapped nervous system and genes that resemble many human genes. This review explains why that worm is useful for studying how nerve cells age and how brain diseases might start.

ocar.opportunity: Postural control—detecting and correcting a bad body orientation—is widespread, yet the circuits that implement it remain poorly resolved in most species.
ocar.challenge: Drosophila larvae perform a stereotyped self-righting maneuver known to need LT1/2 motor neurons and several Hox-targeting microRNAs, but the sensory-to-motor architecture along the body axis had not been mapped and tested.
ocar.action: Picao-Osorio, Roseby, Hancock, Cardona, and Alonso combine connectomics with thermogenetic silencing, starting from LT1/2 motor neurons to identify premotor interneurons, upstream partners, and class IV multidendritic sensory neurons.
ocar.resolution: Inhibiting the great majority of these elements impairs self-righting. The circuit overlaps nociceptive rolling and touch crawling, sharing interneurons including DnB, A02o (Wave-1), and TePn05. Network analyses show hub-like organization, a few integrator neurons bridging sensory and motor subnetworks, and declining synapse number and density toward posterior segments—the first axial wiring diagram for a postural circuit in any animal, the authors state.
ocar.future_work: They suggest hub organization, shared sensory-motor structure, and anteroposterior connectivity gradients may extend to other segmentally organized nervous systems, which remains a comparative hypothesis.

summaries.beginner: When a fruit-fly maggot is flipped onto its back, it can right itself, but the nerve cells that make that happen were only partly known. This study traces those cells from sensors to muscles along the body and shows that turning many of them off makes self-righting worse.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Picao-Osorio, Roseby, Hancock, Cardona, and Alonso map the larval Drosophila self-righting circuit from LT1/2 motor neurons through premotor interneurons to class IV multidendritic sensory neurons. Thermogenetic silencing of most identified elements significantly impairs self-righting. The circuit overlaps rolling and crawling pathways at shared interneurons (DnB, A02o/Wave-1, TePn05). Axial analyses report nested hub-like organization, few integrator neurons, and a posterior decline in synapse number and density. The authors call this the first axial wiring diagram for a postural-control circuit in any animal.
summaries.advanced: “First axial wiring diagram… in any animal” is the authors’ claim; it is not independently validated in the abstract. Silencing “the great majority” of elements impairs performance, which does not by itself prove each cell is uniquely necessary or that the named overlap is causal for rolling/crawling. Posterior synapse-density decline is reported as a structural gradient, not a demonstrated computational necessity.

plain_language_summary: When a fruit-fly maggot is flipped onto its back, it can right itself, but the nerve cells that make that happen were only partly known. This study traces those cells from sensors to muscles along the body and shows that turning many of them off makes self-righting worse.

ocar.opportunity: Deep learning can segment neurons in electron microscopy, which is a path toward reconstructing a connectome.
ocar.challenge: Those models need large, expensive manual annotations, and classic geometric or photometric augmentations stay highly correlated with the original images and lack structural diversity.
ocar.action: Jiang, Zhang, Guo, Han, and colleagues propose a diffusion-based augmentation framework: a resolution-aware conditional diffusion model with multi-scale conditioning and EM resolution priors synthesizes voxel-level images from 3D masks, plus a biology-guided mask remodeling module.
ocar.resolution: On AC3 and AC4 under low-annotation regimes, combining the method with two different post-processing approaches improves the ARAND metric by 32.1% and 30.7%, respectively. Code is released as NeuroDiff.
ocar.future_work: The abstract reports gains in low-annotation settings on two named datasets; transfer to other EM volumes, organisms, or fully unlabeled regimes is not shown here.

summaries.beginner: Computers that outline nerve cells in microscope pictures need many hand-labeled examples, which take a long time to make. This paper uses a modern image-generating model to invent extra realistic training pictures, which helps the computer do a better job when labels are scarce.
summaries.intermediate: At the IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (2026), Jiang, Zhang, Guo, Lu, Zhou, and Han introduce a diffusion-based data-augmentation framework for EM neuron segmentation. A resolution-aware conditional diffusion model with multi-scale conditioning and EM resolution priors synthesizes voxel-level images from 3D masks; a biology-guided module remodels masks for more structural realism. On AC3 and AC4 in low-annotation regimes, the method improves ARAND by 32.1% and 30.7% when combined with two different post-processing methods. Code is at https://github.com/HeadLiuYun/NeuroDiff.
summaries.advanced: Reported ARAND improvements are for low-annotation regimes on AC3 and AC4 and are tied to combination with two post-processing methods; they are not a claim of state-of-the-art on fully labeled public leaderboards. The abstract does not specify which two post-processors or whether gains hold at high annotation counts. Structural “plausibility” of generated pairs is asserted as a design goal of the biology-guided module.

plain_language_summary: Computers that outline nerve cells in microscope pictures need many hand-labeled examples, which take a long time to make. This paper uses a modern image-generating model to invent extra realistic training pictures, which helps the computer do a better job when labels are scarce.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding Alzheimer disease at the subcellular scale is needed to link cellular abnormalities to functional deficits and to guide therapies.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy cannot resolve many of the organelles and filaments implicated in AD, while conventional EM is two-dimensional, fixation-sensitive, and historically focused on plaques and tangles.
ocar.action: Dallere, Migheli, and Vercelli review EM from Terry and Kidd’s 1960s ultrastructure of Aβ deposits and tau paired helical filaments through volume EM, cryo-EM, cryo-ET, and correlated light-EM.
ocar.resolution: These methods enable 3D reconstructions, fewer fixation artifacts, and near-native, near-atomic views, and they have implicated synapses, mitochondria, lysosomes, the blood–brain barrier, iron deposits, and inflammatory machinery. EM work spans human tissue, animal models, cultures, and synthetic assemblies.
ocar.future_work: The review positions EM as a guide for disease-modifying molecule design; it does not itself report a new therapeutic result.

summaries.beginner: Alzheimer disease changes the insides of brain cells in ways too small for ordinary microscopes. This review explains how electron microscopes have shown those tiny changes—from sticky protein clumps to damaged power plants inside cells—and why that still matters for finding treatments.
summaries.intermediate: In Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology (2026), Dallere, Migheli, and Vercelli review electron microscopy in Alzheimer disease research from 1960s descriptions of Aβ deposits and tau paired helical filaments to volume EM, cryo-EM, cryo-ET, and CLEM. They argue these methods yield 3D reconstructions, reduced fixation artifacts, and near-native near-atomic insight, and that EM has revealed roles for synapses, mitochondria, lysosomes, the blood–brain barrier, iron, and inflammation across human tissue, animal models, cultures, and synthetic assemblies. The review frames EM as both a mechanistic and translational tool.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not a new dataset or meta-analysis with effect sizes. “Near-atomic” and “minimize fixation artifacts” describe cryo-EM/ET capabilities in general, not a single quantified AD study in the abstract. Translational language (guiding molecule design) is a stated role for EM, not evidence of a clinical advance.

plain_language_summary: Alzheimer disease changes the insides of brain cells in ways too small for ordinary microscopes. This review explains how electron microscopes have shown those tiny changes—from sticky protein clumps to damaged power plants inside cells—and why that still matters for finding treatments.

ocar.opportunity: Hub scores in multilayer networks might follow a simple rule: they persist more strongly between functionally similar layers than dissimilar ones.
ocar.challenge: Whether that “Functional Proximity Law” is real, where it fails, and whether it appears in connectomes needs pre-registered tests across domains, not a single anecdotal graph.
ocar.action: Ivanov reports 31 pre-registered experiments: 13 canonical domains plus 18 external and replication validations, including a Drosophila melanogaster larval connectome of 2952 neurons.
ocar.resolution: The author reports 25/31 confirmations (binomial p ≈ 0.000439), nine canonical domains at p<0.05, six named boundary conditions including BC_INVERSION, and larval-fly replication with Spearman ρ = 0.663, Pearson r = 0.363, p = 0.002. Additional claimed confirmations include a Standard Model experiment and COBOL banking software.
ocar.future_work: Denied results define six structural boundary conditions, and a predictor Var(d2)<0.714 is offered for BC_RADIAL failure; those boundaries are the natural place to stress-test the law rather than treating it as universal.

summaries.beginner: This paper argues that in stacked networks, important hubs stay important when two layers do similar jobs, and less so when the layers do different jobs. The author tests that idea in many fields, including a fruit-fly larval wiring map, and also lists cases where the idea fails.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 arXiv preprint, Ivanov proposes a Functional Proximity Law: hub-importance scores persist more between functionally similar multilayer-network layers than dissimilar ones. Across 31 pre-registered experiments (13 canonical domains: 10 confirmed, 3 denied; plus 18 external/replication tests: 15 confirmed, 1 denied, 2 partial), the author reports 25/31 confirmations. A Drosophila larval connectome (n = 2952 neurons) is cited as cross-species replication (Spearman ρ = 0.663, Pearson r = 0.363, p = 0.002). Six denied results are named as boundary conditions BC1–BC6.
summaries.advanced: All statistics in the abstract are the author’s pre-registered self-report, spanning particle physics and COBOL as well as neuroscience; independent replication is not described. The fly result is one of many tests, not a full connectomic theory of hubs. Catalog organism is fly; the law is claimed across eight scientific fields. Partial and denied outcomes are acknowledged and turned into named boundary conditions rather than hidden.

plain_language_summary: This paper argues that in stacked networks, important hubs stay important when two layers do similar jobs, and less so when the layers do different jobs. The author tests that idea in many fields, including a fruit-fly larval wiring map, and also lists cases where the idea fails.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans hermaphrodite’s 302-neuron connectome shows how a tiny nervous system can produce adaptive, context-dependent behavior, in contrast to AI systems that often buy performance with scale.
ocar.challenge: Modern artificial networks are typically inefficient relative to biology; it is unclear which worm-circuit principles actually transfer into useful architectures.
ocar.action: Liu, Zheng, and Wang review recent studies that translate C. elegans circuit principles into artificial neural networks for machine control and image classification.
ocar.resolution: Those translations are reported to yield enhanced robustness and improved performance. The mini-review distills a pathway toward compact, adaptive, biologically inspired AI.
ocar.future_work: As a mini-review, it outlines a pathway rather than presenting a new network or benchmark of its own.

summaries.beginner: A tiny worm with only a few hundred nerve cells can still behave in flexible ways. This short review asks what computer scientists can copy from that worm to build smaller, more adaptable artificial networks.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2026), Liu, Zheng, and Wang review how the hermaphroditic C. elegans connectome of 302 neurons has been used as a template for artificial neural networks. They contrast biotic, adaptive worm behavior with AI systems that rely on massive data and engineered scale. Cited translations into machine-control and image-classification architectures are described as improving robustness and performance. The paper offers a pathway toward compact, biologically inspired AI rather than a new model.
summaries.advanced: The 302-neuron figure is the classic hermaphrodite count cited in the abstract; the review does not re-derive the connectome. “Enhanced robustness and improved performance” summarizes cited studies, without numeric results in this abstract. Transfer from nematode circuits to AI remains an analogy-plus-engineering program, not a proof that worm motifs are uniquely optimal.

plain_language_summary: A tiny worm with only a few hundred nerve cells can still behave in flexible ways. This short review asks what computer scientists can copy from that worm to build smaller, more adaptable artificial networks.

ocar.opportunity: In retinitis pigmentosa, inner-retinal remodeling continues after photoreceptor loss, and those wiring changes matter for therapies such as cell replacement, optogenetics, and implants.
ocar.challenge: How Aii amacrine rewiring—especially new gap junctions in the rod pathway—changes signaling is hard to read from anatomy alone.
ocar.action: Iseri, Pfeiffer, Jones, Lazzi, and colleagues extend pathoconnectome analysis of retinal pathoconnectome 1 and build a computational model of the rewired rod network, simulating light-evoked responses and EPSPs.
ocar.resolution: The model predicts significant bipolar and Aii EPSP changes between active and baseline conditions driven by newly formed gap junctions, and rhythmic retinal ganglion cell firing up to 10 Hz. Those predictions align with patch-clamp observations in rd1 and rd10 mice and may relate to impaired photopic–scotopic adaptation.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest extending the model with multi-scale bioelectromagnetic simulations to optimize neurostimulation and to identify therapeutic windows in early degeneration.

summaries.beginner: In some inherited eye diseases, light-sensing cells die and the remaining retinal cells rewire in unusual ways. This study uses a wiring map of a diseased retina plus a computer model to show how those new connections can make output cells fire in a rhythmic, unhealthy pattern.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint (dated 2024.02.14 in the identifier), Iseri, Pfeiffer, Sigulinsky, Anderson, Jones, Lazzi and colleagues analyze Aii amacrine rewiring in retinal pathoconnectome 1 and model the degenerate rod network. Pathoconnectomics shows altered excitatory drive and gap-junctional coupling of Aiis. The model predicts EPSP changes driven by new gap junctions and rhythmic RGC firing up to 10 Hz, consistent with patch-clamp in rd1 and rd10 mouse models of retinitis pigmentosa. The authors propose Aii-mediated alterations as a network cause of atypical RGC firing and as a model for therapy design.
summaries.advanced: Functional consequences are model predictions aligned with published rd1/rd10 physiology, not a new paired recording from the same EM volume. “Up to 10 Hz” is the predicted rhythmic firing rate in the abstract. Catalog datasets are DS09/DS10 mouse retina; the pathoconnectome discussed is RPC1. Therapeutic windows and neurostimulation optimization are proposed extensions.

plain_language_summary: In some inherited eye diseases, light-sensing cells die and the remaining retinal cells rewire in unusual ways. This study uses a wiring map of a diseased retina plus a computer model to show how those new connections can make output cells fire in a rhythmic, unhealthy pattern.

ocar.opportunity: Visual systems are often described as repeating identical units so that the world is sampled uniformly and processing is translationally invariant.
ocar.challenge: Connectomic datasets show that cells assigned to the same type vary in partner identity, partner number, and synapse counts, which sits uneasily with that textbook picture.
ocar.action: Wernet and Silies review regional differences, stochastic microcircuit variation, and this newly visible connectomic heterogeneity in fly visual circuitry.
ocar.resolution: They argue that heterogeneous computations within defined cell types may be the rule rather than the exception.
ocar.future_work: The open question they pose is whether this variability increases functional variability, functional robustness, or both.

summaries.beginner: We often imagine that the eye is built from many identical repeating parts. New wiring maps of the fly visual system show that even cells with the same name do not always connect to the same partners, and this essay asks what that messiness is for.
summaries.intermediate: In BioEssays (2026), Wernet and Silies contrast the classical view of homogeneous, translationally invariant visual modules with connectomic evidence that cells of one type vary in number and identity of partners and in relative synapse numbers. Regional differences and stochastic microcircuit variation had already been linked to specific visual features; whole-circuit maps now show broader heterogeneity. The essay treats heterogeneous computation within cell types as likely the rule and asks whether that raises functional variability or robustness.
summaries.advanced: This is an essay/review, not a new reconstruction. It does not quantify variability or adjudicate variability versus robustness. Catalog fields list no organism or dataset; the title and abstract center on fly visual circuits.

plain_language_summary: We often imagine that the eye is built from many identical repeating parts. New wiring maps of the fly visual system show that even cells with the same name do not always connect to the same partners, and this essay asks what that messiness is for.

ocar.opportunity: Perfusion fixation is widely used to prepare mammalian brain for histology and ultrastructure, including emerging connectomics protocols.
ocar.challenge: Protocols are often judged by gross appearance and neuroimaging of how well perfusate filled the brain, which may not predict ultrastructural preservation.
ocar.action: Slaughter, Garrood, Hedden, McKenzie, and colleagues report three human and one canine brain perfused with fixative containing 10% mannitol and 10% PEG 35 kDa, plus a canine brain with 20% mannitol in 20% NBF without PEG, and compare EM to prior standard-formalin cases.
ocar.resolution: Macroscopic and radiological perfusion quality looked adequate or favorable, but EM showed expanded extracellular space, shrunken processes, and distorted membranes consistent with osmotic shock. Similar artifacts appeared without PEG when mannitol was high.
ocar.future_work: The report warns against optimizing connectomics perfusion protocols on macroscopic or radiological metrics alone, because those metrics can pass while ultrastructure is severely compromised.

summaries.beginner: To study brain tissue under a very powerful microscope, scientists first flush preservative through the blood vessels. This report shows that the brain can look well-preserved to the naked eye and on a scan, yet still be badly shrunk and distorted at the tiny scale that wiring maps need.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv technical report, Slaughter, Garrood, Hedden, Sowa, Janssen, Thorn, De Sanctis, Farrell, Crary, and McKenzie describe hyperosmotic brain perfusion with 10% mannitol and 10% polyethylene glycol 35 kDa in three human donors and one canine donor. Gross and radiological perfusion quality appeared adequate or favorable, but electron microscopy showed expanded extracellular space, shrunken processes, and distorted membranes consistent with osmotic shock. A canine brain with 20% mannitol in 20% neutral buffered formalin without PEG showed similar artifacts, unlike previously reported standard-formalin cases without osmotic additives.
summaries.advanced: This is a small case series (three human, two canine conditions described), not a randomized protocol trial. “Adequate or favorable” macroscopic/radiological quality is qualitative. The causal inference is that dehydrating additives can decouple macro metrics from ultrastructure; the abstract does not report quantitative morphometry of extracellular space. Implications for connectomics are framed as a risk for protocol optimization, not a full human-connectome dataset.

plain_language_summary: To study brain tissue under a very powerful microscope, scientists first flush preservative through the blood vessels. This report shows that the brain can look well-preserved to the naked eye and on a scan, yet still be badly shrunk and distorted at the tiny scale that wiring maps need.

ocar.opportunity: Detergent-free immunolabeling can add molecular identity to volumetric correlated light and electron microscopy, which connectomics needs in order to name cells in ultrastructural volumes.
ocar.challenge: The approach is limited by the supply of suitable small affinity reagents that work without detergents that would wreck membranes.
ocar.action: Lu, Wu, Li, Lichtman, and colleagues introduce CAptVE, using slow off-rate modified aptamers for fluorescent cell labeling on ultrastructurally reconstructable electron micrographs.
ocar.resolution: CAptVE provides labeling for a wide range of biomarkers and a path to integrate molecular analysis into volumetric EM studies of tissues, including neural-circuit connectomics, while preserving ultrastructure.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents a method and pathway rather than a finished brain-wide molecular connectome; expanding the aptamer panel and applying it at circuit scale are the implied next uses.

summaries.beginner: Wiring maps from electron microscopes show cell shape in great detail but often not which molecular type each cell is. This paper introduces chemical tags, called aptamers, that can label many cell types without washing away the membranes the maps depend on.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2026), Lu, Wu, Li, Fang, Schalek, Jain, Janjić, Lichtman and colleagues introduce CAptVE, detergent-free labeling with slow off-rate modified aptamers for fluorescence on ultrastructurally reconstructable EM. Small immunoprobes had already made volumetric CLEM feasible; CAptVE aims to widen the set of biomarkers. The authors position the method as a way to put molecular identity onto large EM volumes, including connectomic circuit reconstructions, while preserving cellular ultrastructure.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report a count of biomarkers, a labeling-density metric, or a named connectome volume. “Wide range of biomarkers” and “at scale” in the journal summary are qualitative. Success still depends on aptamer availability, the original bottleneck the paper seeks to ease.

plain_language_summary: Wiring maps from electron microscopes show cell shape in great detail but often not which molecular type each cell is. This paper introduces chemical tags, called aptamers, that can label many cell types without washing away the membranes the maps depend on.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can place cells, tissues, and circuits in native 3D context, but many specimens are too large to image exhaustively at nanometer resolution.
ocar.challenge: Researchers are forced to choose between broad anatomical context and ultrastructural detail in a single pass.
ocar.action: Chandok, Patel, Wu, Berger, Schalek, Lichtman, Samuel, and Meirovitch introduce random-access electron microscopy (RAEM): a lower-resolution 3D survey, then human- or AI-guided return of the beam to selected physical sites using reconstructed coordinates.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate vesicle-resolved imaging of synaptic boutons in human cortex, targeted imaging of more than one million human cortical mitochondria, hierarchical imaging of a nematode nervous system, and retrospective targeting of a previously published petabyte-scale human cortical volume. Serial-section EM becomes a query-driven, multi-resolution method.
ocar.future_work: The framework is demonstrated on several use cases; turning RAEM into a routine survey-then-query pipeline for other organs and questions is the implied extension.

summaries.beginner: Some pieces of tissue are too big to photograph everywhere at the highest microscope zoom. This method first takes a coarser 3D survey, then sends the electron beam back only to the spots a person or computer wants to see in fine detail.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Chandok, Patel, Wu, Berger, Schalek, Lichtman, Samuel, and Meirovitch describe random-access electron microscopy (RAEM). A lower-resolution 3D survey guides the microscope back to selected sites by linking reconstructed coordinates to beam positions on the original sections. Demonstrations include vesicle-resolved synaptic boutons in human cortex, targeted imaging of more than one million human cortical mitochondria, hierarchical imaging of a nematode nervous system, and retrospective targeting of a published petabyte-scale human cortical volume.
summaries.advanced: “More than one million” mitochondria is the count given in the abstract; completeness of that census and error rates are not reported here. Retrospective targeting of a petabyte-scale volume is a capability claim, not a full reanalysis in the abstract. Catalog organism is listed as human and dataset as C. elegans; the abstract includes both human cortex and a nematode nervous system.

plain_language_summary: Some pieces of tissue are too big to photograph everywhere at the highest microscope zoom. This method first takes a coarser 3D survey, then sends the electron beam back only to the spots a person or computer wants to see in fine detail.

ocar.opportunity: Growing work on the C. elegans male is clarifying how biological sex sculpts a compact nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Sex differences mix extra cell types, rewired synapses, and physiological modulation in ways that are easy to conflate.
ocar.action: Portman, Bainbridge, Ward, and Zhang organize recent findings into three overlapping principles.
ocar.resolution: Sex modulates developmental programs to generate sex-limited neurons and structures; it modifies synaptic topology; and it acts as a dimension of internal state that tunes sex-shared neurons. Together these effects program sex-specific behaviors, tune shared behaviors, and implement sexually dimorphic plasticity, at uniquely high mechanistic resolution in the worm.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that sex-determination mechanisms differ markedly by species, while arguing the three principles are likely conserved—an evolutionary claim to test outside nematodes.

summaries.beginner: Male and female nervous systems can differ even when they share many of the same cells. This essay uses the worm C. elegans to sort those differences into three kinds: extra cell types in one sex, different wiring, and the same cells running in a different internal state.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2026), Portman, Bainbridge, Ward, and Zhang review sexual dimorphism in the C. elegans nervous system. They group effects of biological sex into (1) modulation of lineage, neurogenesis, and cell-fate programs that create sex-limited neurons, (2) modified synaptic connectivity, and (3) sex as a developmental and dynamic internal-state variable in sex-shared neurons. These effects are said to program sex-specific behaviors, tune shared behaviors, and implement dimorphic plasticity. The worm is highlighted for mechanistic resolution; conservation is proposed despite divergent sex-determination mechanisms.
summaries.advanced: This is a current-opinion synthesis, not a new connectome. Conservation of the three principles across species is explicitly a likelihood claim while sex-determination mechanisms “differ markedly.” No quantitative comparison of male versus hermaphrodite synapse counts appears in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Male and female nervous systems can differ even when they share many of the same cells. This essay uses the worm C. elegans to sort those differences into three kinds: extra cell types in one sex, different wiring, and the same cells running in a different internal state.

ocar.opportunity: Data-driven spiking networks can analyze brains at cellular and synaptic resolution, but mammalian models are hard to specify precisely and are computationally heavy.
ocar.challenge: Topology is often statistical, regional function can be unclear, and simulations may need huge facilities and run slower than real time.
ocar.action: Nanami, Yamada, Someya, Hige, Kazama, and Kohno build a lightweight qualitative spiking model of the Drosophila olfactory system with topology taken from connectome data, then implement it on a small entry-level FPGA.
ocar.resolution: The FPGA simulates network activity in real time and the model reproduces olfactory associative learning plus characteristic spiking of different neuron types. The authors present a construction method that is lightweight, hardware-accelerable, and potentially scalable.
ocar.future_work: They suggest the approach could scale to larger networks and may later apply to edge AI; those are stated prospects, not results in this paper.

summaries.beginner: Computer models of brains are often huge and slow. This team built a smaller model of the fruit fly’s smell circuit from real wiring data and ran it in real time on a modest custom chip, reproducing simple learning and typical nerve-cell firing.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2024), Nanami, Yamada, Someya, Hige, Kazama, and Kohno present a lightweight data-driven spiking neuronal network of the Drosophila olfactory system. Topology is extracted from connectome data; neuron dynamics use a qualitative modeling approach. Implemented on a small entry-level FPGA, the model runs in real time and reproduces olfactory associative learning and characteristic spiking of different neuron types. The authors argue the method balances simplicity and reproducibility and is acceleratable in hardware.
summaries.advanced: “Reproduce” learning and characteristic spiking is a qualitative claim in the abstract without numeric error or spike-train metrics. FPGA real-time performance is asserted for this network size, not benchmarked against GPU/CPU equivalents here. Scalability to large-scale networks and edge AI is prospective. Catalog stages include modeling and graph analysis on fly.

plain_language_summary: Computer models of brains are often huge and slow. This team built a smaller model of the fruit fly’s smell circuit from real wiring data and ran it in real time on a modest custom chip, reproducing simple learning and typical nerve-cell firing.

ocar.opportunity: Hungry animals must keep flexible brain function even as modulation reconfigures circuits toward resource seeking.
ocar.challenge: In Drosophila, hunger inhibits aversively reinforcing dopaminergic neurons to allow food-seeking memories, which might undermine aversive learning if uncompensated.
ocar.action: Meschi, Duquenoy, Otto, Dempsey, and Waddell combine behavior, endocrine genetics, and connectomics to trace how adipokinetic hormone (AKH) preserves aversive reinforcement during hunger.
ocar.resolution: Chronic hunger mildly enhances aversive learning; satiated-baseline and hunger-enhanced learning both require AKH signaling via its receptor in four ventral-brain neurons, two of them octopaminergic. Those neurons sit upstream of ascending cells that are presynaptic to aversive DANs; octopaminergic modulation of at least one ascending pathway is required for shock- and bitter-reinforced learning. Coordinated enhancement of input is proposed to compensate hunger-directed DAN inhibition.
ocar.future_work: The compensation hypothesis is the authors’ proposed circuit logic; how fully it generalizes across reinforcers or hunger durations is not settled in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: When an animal is hungry, brain circuits shift toward finding food, which might be expected to weaken learning about danger. This fruit-fly study finds that a hormone helps keep punishment learning working by boosting input to the same cells that hunger otherwise quiets.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2024), Meschi, Duquenoy, Otto, Dempsey, and Waddell show that chronic hunger mildly enhances Drosophila aversive learning and that both baseline and hunger-enhanced learning require adipokinetic hormone (AKH). Circulating AKH acts via receptors in four ventral-brain neurons, two octopaminergic. Connectomics places AKH-receptor neurons upstream of ascending neurons that are presynaptic to aversively reinforcing dopaminergic neurons. Octopaminergic modulation of at least one ascending pathway is required for shock- and bitter-taste-reinforced learning. The authors propose coordinated input enhancement compensates hunger-directed inhibition of aversive DANs.
summaries.advanced: “Mildly enhances” is the abstract’s qualifier for hunger’s effect on aversive learning; no numeric effect size is given. The compensation account is a proposed circuit logic supported by genetics, behavior, and connectivity, not a direct demonstration that input gain quantitatively offsets DAN inhibition. Two of four AKH-receptor neurons are identified as octopaminergic; the other two are not typed in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: When an animal is hungry, brain circuits shift toward finding food, which might be expected to weaken learning about danger. This fruit-fly study finds that a hormone helps keep punishment learning working by boosting input to the same cells that hunger otherwise quiets.

ocar.opportunity: Rat stroke and hemorrhage models are workhorses for cerebrovascular pathophysiology, but how functional impairment maps onto connectivity change at neuronal-population and mesoscopic scales is unresolved.
ocar.challenge: Lesions differ in extent and location across models, so relating motor and memory deficits to network architecture requires a common connectome framework.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, Wang, Kanoke, Rabiller, and Liu compare two middle-cerebral-artery occlusion models and one intracerebral-hemorrhage model, assessing motor and spatial memory, hippocampal Fos, and connectivity change on the neuroVIISAS rat connectome, plus dynamic coactivation modeling.
ocar.resolution: Impairment correlated with both extent and location of injury. Lesioned regions coactivated more strongly with motor and spatial-learning regions than with other unaffected nodes. Weighted bilateral dynamic modeling detected remote hippocampal signal-propagation changes in all three stroke types, predicting the extent of hippocampal hypoactivation and spatial-memory impairment.
ocar.future_work: The authors offer the pipeline as a framework for predictive identification of remote regions not directly hit by the lesion; applying it to other species or human stroke connectomes is outside this abstract.

summaries.beginner: A stroke damages one patch of brain, but problems with movement or memory can come from far-away regions that were only indirectly affected. This rat study uses a whole-brain wiring map and computer simulations to predict which distant areas will slow down after different kinds of stroke.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2024), Schmitt, Eipert, Wang, Kanoke, Rabiller, and Liu study two MCAO models and one intracerebral-hemorrhage model in rat. Motor and spatial memory, hippocampal Fos activation, and connectome-based measures (connection similarity, graph and spatial distance, regional importance on the neuroVIISAS rat connectome) are combined with coactivation analysis in dynamic brain models. Functional impairment correlated with injury extent and location. Dynamic modeling with the weighted bilateral connectome detected remote hippocampal changes in all three stroke types, predicting hippocampal hypoactivation and spatial-learning/memory impairment.
summaries.advanced: Predictions of remote hippocampal effects are from dynamic modeling on a literature-derived rat connectome, validated against Fos and behavior in these models, not from new tract-tracing of each lesion. Catalog organism is “other” (rat). The abstract does not report sample sizes or statistical thresholds.

plain_language_summary: A stroke damages one patch of brain, but problems with movement or memory can come from far-away regions that were only indirectly affected. This rat study uses a whole-brain wiring map and computer simulations to predict which distant areas will slow down after different kinds of stroke.

ocar.opportunity: Co-active or temporally ordered ensembles mark salient events; if their axons clustered on dendrites, single neurons could use dendritic nonlinearities to decode those patterns.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether such clustered convergence is likely even in randomly connected networks, or whether it requires special wiring.
ocar.action: Somashekar and Bhalla combine theory and simulations using rat hippocampal and cortical network statistics to estimate clustered and sequential axonal convergence onto synaptic clusters.
ocar.resolution: Clustered convergence from 3–4 co-active ensembles is likely even at random, representing arbitrary input combinations in at least ten target neurons in a 100,000-cell population. With larger ensembles, spatiotemporally ordered convergence of 3–5 axons is also likely. Active clusters raise neuronal activation when dendritic nonlinearities are strong and background activity is low.
ocar.future_work: They conclude that clustered and sequence computation is pervasive but that somatic selectivity requires a confluence of physiology, background activity, and connectomics—an interplay to test in identified circuits, not only in random-network models.

summaries.beginner: Groups of brain cells often fire together, and a single receiving cell might notice that pattern if those inputs land in a tight cluster on its branches. This modeling paper argues that such clusters can appear even when connections are random, but the cell’s output will only look selective under the right background conditions.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Somashekar and Bhalla use theory and simulations with rat hippocampal and cortical network statistics to ask whether ensemble axons converge as dendritic synaptic clusters in randomly connected feedforward networks. Clustered convergence from 3–4 co-active ensembles is likely at random, yielding representation of arbitrary combinations in at least ten neurons per 100,000. With larger ensembles, ordered convergence of 3–5 axons is also likely. Cluster-driven activation is stronger with strong dendritic nonlinearities and low background activity.
summaries.advanced: The “at least ten in 100,000” figure is a model result under stated random-connectivity statistics, not an empirical count from reconstructions. Catalog organism is “other.” Expression of clustered computation as somatic selectivity is explicitly conditional on physiology, background activity, and connectomics; the paper does not claim random wiring is sufficient for reliable decoding in vivo.

plain_language_summary: Groups of brain cells often fire together, and a single receiving cell might notice that pattern if those inputs land in a tight cluster on its branches. This modeling paper argues that such clusters can appear even when connections are random, but the cell’s output will only look selective under the right background conditions.

ocar.opportunity: The circadian clock times physiology, but how temperature reorganizes clock-dependent activity and sleep is not fully mapped in a central circuit.
ocar.challenge: Identifying which clock neurons sense temperature and how they split influence over locomotion versus sleep requires combined in vivo imaging, anatomy, and behavior.
ocar.action: Li, Li, Yuan, Guo, and colleagues use in-vivo two-photon imaging with temperature control, trans-synaptic tracing, connectome analysis, and behavior in Drosophila.
ocar.resolution: DN1as are the most sensitive temperature-sensing neurons among those examined; the clock gates their diurnal temperature response. DN1as bidirectionally target activity-related E cells and sleep-promoting DN3s. DN1a–E cells modulate the evening locomotion peak in cold, while DN1a–DN3 cells control warm-induced nocturnal sleep reduction.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest these motifs may illuminate conserved temperature-regulated circadian physiology; conservation is not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Body clocks keep daily rhythms, but temperature also changes when an animal is active or asleep. In fruit flies, this study finds a pair of clock cells that feel temperature and send opposite messages: one path adjusts evening movement in the cold, another reduces night sleep when it is warm.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024), Li, Li, Yuan, Tian, Ye, Zeng, Li, and Guo combine in-vivo two-photon imaging, temperature control, trans-synaptic tracing, connectome analysis, and behavior in Drosophila. DN1as emerge as the most sensitive temperature-sensing neurons in the central circadian circuit; the clock gates their diurnal temperature response. DN1as bidirectionally target activity-related E cells and sleep-promoting DN3s. Behavior shows the DN1a–E circuit modulates the evening locomotion peak in cold, and the DN1a–DN3 circuit controls warm-temperature nocturnal sleep reduction.
summaries.advanced: “Most sensitive” is among neurons imaged in this central-circuit survey, not a claim about all thermosensors in the fly. Bidirectional targeting is supported by tracing, connectome analysis, and functional imaging as listed; the abstract does not give synapse counts. Conservation of the mechanism in other animals is suggested, not shown. Catalog stages include proofreading and method two-photon.

plain_language_summary: Body clocks keep daily rhythms, but temperature also changes when an animal is active or asleep. In fruit flies, this study finds a pair of clock cells that feel temperature and send opposite messages: one path adjusts evening movement in the cold, another reduces night sleep when it is warm.

ocar.opportunity: Instance segmentation of neurons in volumetric light microscopy would let researchers jointly study function and morphology at cellular resolution.
ocar.challenge: Neurons are long, thin, branching, and tightly interwoven; light-microscopy artifacts (partial volume, uneven illumination, noise) make local disentangling and long-range tracing hard, and machine-learning methods for long-range dependencies are usually benchmarked on synthetic data.
ocar.action: Mais, Hirsch, Kainmüller, and colleagues release FISBe, a public multi-neuron light-microscopy dataset with pixel-wise annotations, plus task-specific instance-segmentation metrics and three baselines.
ocar.resolution: FISBe is presented as the first publicly available multi-neuron light-microscopy dataset with pixel-wise annotations, intended to drive methods that capture long-range dependencies and to aid basic neuroscience.
ocar.future_work: The dataset is meant to seed a competition; how well winners transfer to other microscopes, species, or denser brains is left to that community process.

summaries.beginner: Computers still struggle to outline individual nerve cells in 3D light-microscope pictures because the cells are thin, long, and tangled. This paper releases a real annotated dataset so that new computer methods can be tested fairly, not only on fake images.
summaries.intermediate: At Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (2024), Mais, Hirsch, Managan, Kandarpa, Rumberger, Reinke, Maier-Hein, Ihrke, and Kainmüller release the FlyLight Instance Segmentation Benchmark (FISBe). They argue that multi-neuron light microscopy combines long-range thin processes, interweaving, and imaging artifacts that current methods rarely face on synthetic benchmarks. The release includes pixel-wise annotations, instance-segmentation metrics designed for downstream analyses, and three baselines. A project page is provided to host a competition.
summaries.advanced: “First publicly available” is the authors’ claim for pixel-wise annotated multi-neuron LM. Metrics are designed to be meaningful for downstream analyses, but the abstract does not list numeric baseline scores. Catalog stages include segmentation, proofreading, and graph analysis; the paper itself is a vision benchmark, not a connectome reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Computers still struggle to outline individual nerve cells in 3D light-microscope pictures because the cells are thin, long, and tangled. This paper releases a real annotated dataset so that new computer methods can be tested fairly, not only on fake images.

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy now yields detailed local connectivity, while MRI-scale imaging speaks to inter-regional links; relating the two in health and disease needs cell-level long-range axons.
ocar.challenge: Whole-brain axonal reconstructions remain sparse relative to the number of neurons, so a brain-wide single-cell connectome cannot be measured directly from those data alone.
ocar.action: Petkantchin, Berchet, Peng, Markram, and Kanari present a method to generate detailed whole-brain axonal morphologies from sparse experimental reconstructions and thereby predict whole-brain connectivity at single-cell level.
ocar.resolution: Computationally generated axons are reported to reproduce local and global morphological properties of experimental reconstructions and to define large-scale inter-regional projectome and connectome structure for in silico experiments on large brain regions.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents a generation technique rather than a fully validated all-species atlas; testing how well synthetic axons predict held-out reconstructions and disease-altered brains is the natural next measurement.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can reconstruct a few neurons’ long-distance cables in great detail, but not every cell in a whole brain. This paper describes a way to grow realistic extra cables in the computer from those examples so that large-scale wiring can be studied in simulation.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint (DOI pointing at a later Nature Communications version), Petkantchin, Berchet, Peng, Markram, and Kanari generate whole-brain axonal morphologies from sparse experimental reconstructions. They report that synthetic axons reproduce local and global morphological properties of the experimental set and yield large-scale inter-regional connectivity—a projectome and connectome—for in silico experiments on large brain regions. The motivation is bridging EM-scale local connectivity and MRI-scale inter-regional maps.
summaries.advanced: Fidelity is described as accurate reproduction of morphological properties, without numeric error metrics in the abstract. Species and brain region of the “novel dataset” of whole-brain axonal reconstructions are not named in the abstract. Catalog method is electron microscopy and year/journal fields list 2024 bioRxiv despite a Nature Communications-style DOI on the record.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can reconstruct a few neurons’ long-distance cables in great detail, but not every cell in a whole brain. This paper describes a way to grow realistic extra cables in the computer from those examples so that large-scale wiring can be studied in simulation.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-resolution fly connectomes across developmental stages make it possible to ask how connection probability scales with physical distance at cellular resolution.
ocar.challenge: Coarse-grained brain networks had been described with an exponential distance rule; whether neuron-level wiring follows the same law, and whether that law is functionally meaningful, was open.
ocar.action: Zhang, Moore, Ru, and Yan analyze fruit-fly synapse-resolution connectomes across developmental stages and compare geometric scaling to information-theoretic and criticality criteria, then perturb the probability model.
ocar.resolution: They report a consistent power-law scaling of connection probability with distance, unlike the exponential distance rule of coarse-grained networks. The scaling aligns with maximum entropy of communication and a criticality balance of integration and segregation; perturbing model parameters or type loses those properties. They also derive a predictor of connectivity from distance plus in- and out-degree.
ocar.future_work: The abstract links geometry to topology and optimal operation in confined space; whether the same power law holds in other species’ synapse-resolution maps is not shown here.

summaries.beginner: Nearby brain cells are more likely to connect than far-apart ones, but the exact rule can differ when you look at single synapses versus large brain regions. This study of fruit-fly wiring finds a simple distance rule at the synapse scale and argues that the rule helps the network share information efficiently.
summaries.intermediate: In Physical Review Letters (2024), Zhang, Moore, Ru, and Yan report that synapse-resolution fruit-fly connectomes across developmental stages show a power-law scaling of neuronal connection probability with spatial distance, distinct from the exponential distance rule of coarse-grained networks. They argue the geometric law aligns with maximum entropy of information communication and functional criticality balancing integration and segregation. Perturbing the empirical probability model’s parameters or type removes those properties. An explicit predictor uses only interneuronal distance and in- and out-degree.
summaries.advanced: The contrast with the exponential distance rule is to prior coarse-grained observations, not a re-fit of those datasets in the abstract. Alignment with maximum entropy and criticality is a reported functional significance of the scaling, tested by perturbation of the probability model. Developmental stages are mentioned but not listed. Catalog stages: graph analysis; no organism tag on the row, but the abstract specifies fruit flies.

plain_language_summary: Nearby brain cells are more likely to connect than far-apart ones, but the exact rule can differ when you look at single synapses versus large brain regions. This study of fruit-fly wiring finds a simple distance rule at the synapse scale and argues that the rule helps the network share information efficiently.

ocar.opportunity: Turning image volumes into 3D geometries and skeletons of neurons is a bottleneck for brain function, connectomics, and pathology, and domain scientists need topologically exact complete segmentations.
ocar.challenge: Existing reconstruction methods are disk-bound, dense-access, coupled, single-threaded, algorithmically unscalable, and typically require cropping small windows and heavy skeleton proofreading.
ocar.action: Marrett, Moradi, Park, Cong, and colleagues present Gossamer, recasting vision tasks as strategically ordered specializations of search to cut memory and enable whole-brain processing.
ocar.resolution: The approach is reported to lower memory by 4 orders of magnitude, allowing one mouse brain to be fully processed in-memory on a single server, at 67× the scale with 870× less memory and 78% higher automated yield than APP2, described as the previous state of the art in performant reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: Comparisons in the abstract are to APP2 on the mouse-brain scale claimed; generalization to other species, EM versus light microscopy, and remaining proofreading burden are not quantified here.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every nerve cell in a whole-brain picture usually takes too much computer memory and a lot of hand correction. This software redesigns the tracing job so that a full mouse brain can be processed in the memory of a single server, with less cleanup than a leading older method.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Marrett, Moradi, Park, Yan, Choi, Zhu, and colleagues introduce Gossamer for scaling neuronal reconstruction to whole brains. They argue prior methods are disk-bound, dense-access, single-threaded, and topologically inaccurate enough to force cropping and skeleton proofreading. By ordering specializations of search, they report a 4-order-of-magnitude memory reduction. One mouse brain is fully processed in-memory on a single server at 67× the scale, 870× less memory, and 78% higher automated yield than APP2.
summaries.advanced: The 67× / 870× / 78% figures are relative to APP2 as stated in the abstract; the comparison set is not a multi-algorithm public leaderboard. “Fully processed” and “automated yield” are the authors’ terms; residual topological error after automation is not given. Catalog organism is mouse; imaging modality is not named in the abstract (neuronal reconstruction from image volumes).

plain_language_summary: Tracing every nerve cell in a whole-brain picture usually takes too much computer memory and a lot of hand correction. This software redesigns the tracing job so that a full mouse brain can be processed in the memory of a single server, with less cleanup than a leading older method.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy is the method of choice for in situ cellular ultrastructure at nanometer scale, and datasets are growing faster than manual analysis.
ocar.challenge: Life-science users with modest computational expertise need organelle-specific 3D labels, spatial analysis, and visualization on a standard workstation, with as little annotation as possible.
ocar.action: Müller, Schmidt, Albrecht, Weigert, and colleagues describe a modular pipeline using freely available tools (Microscopy Image Browser, ilastik, Labkit, Album-wrapped CSBDeep, CellSketch, StarDist, Blender, Jupyter) plus Album solutions that bridge compatibility gaps.
ocar.resolution: The protocol covers raw-data preparation, organelle segmentation, spatial analysis, and 3D visualization, with guidelines for choosing segmentation tools per organelle, runnable on a single-user workstation.
ocar.future_work: The write-up is a protocol for similar single- or multiple-organelle projects; it does not itself introduce a new learning architecture or a public segmented atlas.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope volumes are hard to turn into 3D maps of cell parts if you are not a software engineer. This protocol walks biologists through free tools that label organelles, measure how they sit next to each other, and display the result on an ordinary computer.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Protocols (2024), Müller, Schmidt, Albrecht, Rieckert, Otto, Galicia Garcia, Fabig, Solimena, and Weigert present a modular, annotation-efficient pipeline for segmentation, spatial analysis, and visualization of volume EM on a standard workstation. Tools include Microscopy Image Browser, ilastik, Labkit, and Album-packaged Python software (CSBDeep, CellSketch, StarDist, Blender, Jupyter notebooks). The protocol targets life-science users with modest computational expertise and provides guidelines for choosing organelle-specific segmentation tools.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods protocol, not a benchmark claiming superior accuracy versus other segmenters. “Annotation-efficient” and “single standard workstation” are design constraints, without dataset sizes or GPU/CPU timings in the abstract. Album is used to mitigate compatibility issues among open-source tools—an engineering caveat for long-term reproducibility.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope volumes are hard to turn into 3D maps of cell parts if you are not a software engineer. This protocol walks biologists through free tools that label organelles, measure how they sit next to each other, and display the result on an ordinary computer.

ocar.opportunity: Synapses are often precisely organized on dendrites, but how that topography shapes dendritic integration is poorly understood.
ocar.challenge: Relating synapse placement to integration requires both EM-precise locations and models fitted to physiology.
ocar.action: Moreno-Sanchez, Vasserman, Jang, von Reyn, Ausborn, and colleagues use EM connectomics of Drosophila looming circuits, focusing on retinotopic visual projection neurons onto descending neurons, plus multicompartment DN models with precise morphologies and synapse locations.
ocar.resolution: A given VPN type projects to non-overlapping regions on DN dendrites; within those clusters, synapses are not retinotopic but near random. DN dendrite morphologies normalize individual EPSP amplitudes, and near-random synapse distributions ensure linear encoding of synapse numbers from individual VPNs.
ocar.future_work: They suggest linear encoding of synapse numbers may be a default set by connectivity and passive properties, on which active properties and plasticity can later tune—an idea to test with perturbations of those active mechanisms.

summaries.beginner: Where contacts sit on a cell’s branches can change how that cell adds up incoming messages. In fruit-fly neurons that trigger escape from approaching objects, this study finds contacts from one partner type sit in a neighborhood but are shuffled inside it, which helps the cell count those contacts in a simple, linear way.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Moreno-Sanchez, Vasserman, Jang, Hina, von Reyn, and Ausborn analyze EM connectomes of Drosophila looming-responsive visual projection neurons synapsing onto descending neurons. Synapses of a given VPN type occupy non-overlapping DN dendritic territories but are near randomly placed within those territories rather than retinotopically ordered. Multicompartment models fitted to experimental data and using EM morphologies and synapse locations indicate that DN dendrite shape normalizes individual EPSPs and that near-random placement supports linear encoding of VPN synapse numbers.
summaries.advanced: “Near random” is the authors’ description of intra-cluster topography, not a formal statistical test named in the abstract. Linear encoding is a model result under fitted passive properties; the abstract presents active properties and plasticity as subsequent tuners, not included as the default. Catalog organism is fly; method electron microscopy; stage graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Where contacts sit on a cell’s branches can change how that cell adds up incoming messages. In fruit-fly neurons that trigger escape from approaching objects, this study finds contacts from one partner type sit in a neighborhood but are shuffled inside it, which helps the cell count those contacts in a simple, linear way.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic reconstruction from EM usually starts with automatic segmentation that is mostly over-segmented, then relies on expert proofreading.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading large neuron populations is slow if humans must search without ranked merge candidates.
ocar.action: Liu, Chen, and Chen present NeuProofreader, which extracts potential segment pairs, predicts pairwise connectivity from morphology and EM features, and exposes 2D image and 3D mesh views with interactive selection.
ocar.resolution: Combining deep-learning suggestions with manual inspection is reported to accelerate reconstruction and enhance accuracy. Code is released on GitHub.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not report timed user studies or accuracy deltas; those measurements on public volumes would be the natural evaluation.

summaries.beginner: Computers split microscope volumes into pieces of nerve cells, but people still have to glue the pieces together. This software suggests which pieces likely belong to the same cell and lets a person accept or reject those suggestions while looking at pictures and 3D shapes.
summaries.intermediate: At the 2024 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo Workshops, Liu, Chen, and Chen present NeuProofreader, an interactive proofreading system for connectomics. An algorithm extracts potential neuron-segment pairs and predicts pairwise connectivity from morphology and EM image features. The interface provides 2D image and 3D mesh visualization and interactive segment selection. The authors state that combining automatic predictions with manual inspection significantly accelerates reconstruction and enhances accuracy; code is at GitHub.
summaries.advanced: “Significantly accelerates” and “enhances accuracy” are not accompanied by numeric benchmarks, dataset names, or inter-rater statistics in the abstract. The pipeline assumes mostly over-segmented automatic input. The GitHub URL in the abstract appears to contain a typographically odd username; users should verify the repository path.

plain_language_summary: Computers split microscope volumes into pieces of nerve cells, but people still have to glue the pieces together. This software suggests which pieces likely belong to the same cell and lets a person accept or reject those suggestions while looking at pictures and 3D shapes.

ocar.opportunity: A human nanoscale connectome requires a synaptome: morphology and storage estimates for every synapse as the substrate of microcircuits and of mental capacity and disorders.
ocar.challenge: Literature values for neuron and synapse counts span a wide range, so storage needs depend on both biology and how much geometry each synapse record stores.
ocar.action: Nowinski defines a synapse as paired pre/post neuron and terminal identifiers with optional coordinates and radii, then estimates storage for three models (topologic, point, geometric), full and simplified, across four neuron counts (30, 86, 100, 138 billion) and three synapses-per-neuron values (1,000; 10,000; 30,000)—72 cases.
ocar.resolution: Whole-brain full (simplified) storage ranges from 0.21 (0.14) PB to 28.98 (18.63) PB (topologic), 0.57 (0.32)–78.66 (43.47) PB (point), and 0.69 (0.38)–95.22 (51.75) PB (geometric). Cortical ranges are given down to tens of TB. The topologic model suffices for connectome topology but is still too large for today’s top neuroscience supercomputers; Frontier could handle 86 billion neurons at 1,000–10,000 synapses per neuron.
ocar.future_work: The author presents this as a first big-data storage estimate, not a measured human synaptome; actual nanoscale mapping would still have to choose a model and live with biological count uncertainty.

summaries.beginner: Writing down every tiny contact in a human brain would take an enormous amount of computer storage, and nobody is sure how many contacts there are. This paper estimates the disk space needed under different counting assumptions and different amounts of detail per contact.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2024), Nowinski models the human nanoscale synaptome as paired presynaptic and postsynaptic neuron and terminal identifiers, optionally with coordinates and radii.
