Three models (topologic, point, geometric), each full or simplified, are crossed with four neuron counts (30; 86; 100; 138 billion) and three synapses-per-neuron values (1,000; 10,000; 30,000). Whole-brain estimates span 0.21–95.22 petabytes depending on model and counts; cortical estimates span 86.80 TB–8.56 PB. The topologic model is said to suffice for topology but still exceeds typical neuroscience supercomputers; Frontier could handle 86 billion neurons at 1,000–10,000 synapses per neuron.
summaries.advanced: All numeric ranges are combinatorial estimates from literature count brackets, not measurements. The claim that this is the first such storage estimate is the author’s. “Too big to be stored on today’s top supercomputers related to neuroscience” is qualified by the Frontier exception for a subset of cases. Catalog stages: infrastructure, graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Writing down every tiny contact in a human brain would take an enormous amount of computer storage, and nobody is sure how many contacts there are. This paper estimates the disk space needed under different counting assumptions and different amounts of detail per contact.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping connectivity of diverse neuronal types at cellular resolution and brain-wide scale needs high-throughput, lower-cost neuroanatomy.
ocar.challenge: Sindbis barcode methods are anterograde and long-range; rabies can do retrograde labeling and monosynaptic tracing, but barcoded rabies had been used mainly for non-neuronal interactions in vivo and cultured neurons, not mouse-brain circuits at scale.
ocar.action: Zhang, Jin, Yao, Chen, and colleagues combine barcoded rabies with single-cell RNA-seq and in situ sequencing in mouse to perform retrograde and transsynaptic labeling.
ocar.resolution: They sequenced 96 retrogradely and 295 transsynaptically labeled cells by scRNA-seq, and 4130 retrogradely and 2914 transsynaptically labeled cells in situ. Transcriptomic identities of infected cells were robustly recovered. Linking gene expression to barcode-inferred connectivity distinguished long-range cortical projection types and cell types with converging or diverging synapses.
ocar.future_work: They present a potential path for mapping synaptic connectivity of neuronal types at scale; a complete brain-wide type-resolved rabies connectome is not claimed.

summaries.beginner: To see which kinds of brain cells talk to which, scientists can tag cells with genetic barcodes and then read those tags with RNA methods. This mouse study shows that a rabies virus carrying barcodes can both label far-away cells and list their molecular types.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2024), Zhang, Jin, Yao, van Velthoven, Wickersham, Chen and colleagues combine barcoded rabies virus with single-cell RNA-seq and in situ sequencing in mouse brain. They report 96 retrograde and 295 transsynaptic cells by scRNA-seq, and 4130 retrograde and 2914 transsynaptic cells in situ. Transcriptomic identities of rabies-infected cells were robustly identified with both readouts. Associating gene expression with barcode-inferred connectivity distinguished long-range projecting cortical types and types with converging or diverging synaptic connectivity.
summaries.advanced: Cell counts are the sequenced labeled populations, not a saturation of all inputs to a region. “Robustly identified” transcriptomic identity is the authors’ assessment; the abstract does not give classification accuracy. Rabies biology (toxicity, tropism, skip of some synapses) is not discussed in the abstract and remains a general caveat for monosynaptic tracing. Catalog stage is proofreading; the work is sequencing-based neuroanatomy.

plain_language_summary: To see which kinds of brain cells talk to which, scientists can tag cells with genetic barcodes and then read those tags with RNA methods. This mouse study shows that a rabies virus carrying barcodes can both label far-away cells and list their molecular types.

ocar.opportunity: Primate visual cortex is modular, hierarchical, spatially arranged around V1, and retinotopic with mirror reversals at area boundaries—an architectural, spatial, and topographic package.
ocar.challenge: The developmental rules that produce all three aspects together are unknown, and it is unclear whether detailed genetic cues for features such as map reversal are required.
ocar.action: Chandra, Khona, Konkle, and Fiete present a synaptic growth rule driven by spontaneous activity and heterosynaptic competition, and identify a theoretical principle of local greedy wiring minimization via spontaneous drive (GWM-S).
ocar.resolution: The rule generates a visual-pathway connectome with modularity, hierarchy, spatial layout, and topographic maps including mirror reversals, without detailed genetic cues for map reversal. Alternative biologically distinct growth rules predict similar endpoints but distinguishable trajectories. The same rules, given input and cortical geometry, predict hierarchical convolution-like pathways across modalities and species.
ocar.future_work: The model yields predictions for normal and perturbed development; those trajectories are proposed experimental tests rather than data already collected here.

summaries.beginner: The visual part of a primate brain is divided into areas that sit in a nested layout and contain flipped maps of the eye. This modeling study shows that a simple growth rule, driven by spontaneous activity and competition between connections, can grow that layout without a detailed genetic blueprint for every flip.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Chandra, Khona, Konkle, and Fiete show that a synaptic growth rule driven by spontaneous activity and heterosynaptic competition can generate modular, hierarchical, spatially arranged, and retinotopic visual pathways with mirror reversals at area boundaries. They formulate local greedy wiring minimization via spontaneous drive (GWM-S) and propose biologically distinct rules with similar endpoints but testably different developmental trajectories. Few parameters act as knobs for projection-neuron-like versus interneuron-like patterns. The same rules are argued to explain pluripotent cortical structure formation across modalities and species given input and cortical geometry.
summaries.advanced: This is a developmental model, not a fit to a measured primate connectome in the abstract. “Without detailed genetic cues for map reversal” is a sufficiency claim for the simulated rule, not evidence that biology lacks such cues. Catalog organism is “other.” Predictions for perturbed development are offered as experimental tests.

plain_language_summary: The visual part of a primate brain is divided into areas that sit in a nested layout and contain flipped maps of the eye. This modeling study shows that a simple growth rule, driven by spontaneous activity and competition between connections, can grow that layout without a detailed genetic blueprint for every flip.

ocar.opportunity: Stroke is a leading cause of adult disability, and recovery depends on how complex brain networks change across spatiotemporal scales.
ocar.challenge: Macroscale readout and network modeling have transformed understanding of large-scale stroke effects, but reorganization of smaller-scale networks remains incomplete.
ocar.action: Latifi and Carmichael review graph-theoretic definitions of brain networks from nano- to macroscales and highlight stroke connectivity studies at multiple scales.
ocar.resolution: They argue that multiscale connectomics-based approaches may provide new routes to evaluate structural and functional remapping after stroke and during recovery.
ocar.future_work: As a review, it advocates a program of multiscale measurement rather than reporting a new cohort or intervention.

summaries.beginner: A stroke changes more than one spot in the brain: it changes how many scales of networks talk to each other. This review argues that mapping those networks from tiny connections up to whole-brain scans could better explain recovery.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Neurosciences (2024), Latifi and Carmichael review stroke through a graph-theory framework spanning nano- to macroscale networks. They note that brain readout technologies and complex-network modeling have clarified macroscale effects, while smaller-scale reorganization remains incompletely understood. Highlighting multi-scale connectivity studies, they argue that multiscale connectomics may offer new routes to evaluate structural and functional remapping after stroke and during recovery.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinionated review, not a meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes. “May provide new routes” is a programmatic claim. Catalog stages include infrastructure and graph analysis; no specific organism or dataset is attached.

plain_language_summary: A stroke changes more than one spot in the brain: it changes how many scales of networks talk to each other. This review argues that mapping those networks from tiny connections up to whole-brain scans could better explain recovery.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM now images the same area at high resolution with overlap so that tiles can be stitched into large, high-resolution ultrastructure.
ocar.challenge: When global feature distributions are uneven and overlap features fail to match, fusion regions ghost, and no prior method is described as perfect.
ocar.action: He, Zhang, Zhang, Cheng, Zhang, Sun, and Han develop vEMstitch, combining global rigid and local elastic transforms via weighted pixel displacement fields, plus local geometric constraints and feature re-extraction.
ocar.resolution: On simulated datasets with different transformation combinations the algorithm shows promising performance; on real samples it yields clear ultrastructure in the stitching region. Source code is public.
ocar.future_work: The abstract emphasizes visualization and identification benefits; a large public leaderboard comparison is not reported here.

summaries.beginner: To photograph a large piece of tissue at very high zoom, microscopes take overlapping tiles that must be sewn together. This paper introduces an automatic sewing method meant to avoid blurry double images where the tiles meet.
summaries.intermediate: In GigaScience (2024), He, Zhang, Zhang, Cheng, Zhang, Sun, and Han present vEMstitch for fully automatic volume-EM image stitching. The transform model combines global rigid and local elastic warps using weighted pixel displacement fields, with local geometric constraints and feature re-extraction aimed at biological distortions. Simulated datasets with mixed transforms show promising performance, and real-sample experiments give clear ultrastructure in the stitch region. Code is at https://github.com/HeracleBT/vEMstitch.
summaries.advanced: “Promising performance” on simulations and “clear ultrastructure” on real data are qualitative in the abstract; numeric registration errors are not given. The method targets ghosting when overlap features mismatch due to uneven global feature distributions. Catalog stages include alignment, graph analysis, modeling, and acquisition.

plain_language_summary: To photograph a large piece of tissue at very high zoom, microscopes take overlapping tiles that must be sewn together. This paper introduces an automatic sewing method meant to avoid blurry double images where the tiles meet.

ocar.opportunity: Single-neuron projections are essential for understanding hippocampal connectivity and its many functions, but brain-wide single-cell projectomes had not been assembled at this scale.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear how individual hippocampal neurons broadcast to nearby and distant targets and how soma location specifies those projectomes.
ocar.action: Qiu, Hu, Huang, Poo, Sun, Li, Yao, Gong, Sun, Xu, and colleagues sparsely labeled neurons, imaged with fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography, and reconstructed 10,100 mouse hippocampal single-neuron projectomes, with spatial transcriptomics of hippocampal sections.
ocar.resolution: They classify 43 projectome subtypes (from 341 projection patterns), relate target number and axon-tip distribution to longitudinal and transverse soma position, find enrichment in spatial-transcriptomic subdomains, and report intra-HPF versus extra-HPF wiring diagrams, ipsilateral preference for bihemispheric pairs, and other organizational principles. Data are released with a web interface.
ocar.future_work: The resource is positioned as a structural basis for function and for combining with gene expression to define subtypes; physiology of the 43 subtypes is not mapped here.

summaries.beginner: Hippocampal cells send long branches all over the brain, but those paths had not been drawn for thousands of single cells. This mouse study reconstructs more than ten thousand such cells and sorts them into projection types that depend on where the cell body sits.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2024), Qiu, Hu, Huang, Gao, and a large consortium reconstruct 10,100 single-neuron projectomes of mouse hippocampus using sparse labeling and fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography. Neurons fall into 341 projection patterns and 43 projectome subtypes. Projection-target number and axon-tip distribution depend on soma location along hippocampal longitudinal and transverse axes; many subtypes are enriched in spatial-transcriptomic subdomains. The authors delineate intra-hippocampal-formation versus extra-HPF wiring, ipsilateral preference of bihemispheric projections, and axon-orientation rules for mossy fibers and Schaffer collaterals.
summaries.advanced: 10,100 is the reconstructed count in the abstract; coverage relative to all hippocampal neurons is not given. Classification into 43 subtypes is morphology- and target-based; spatial transcriptomics is correlated with soma location rather than a full single-cell RNA-seq of the same neurons. Function is inferred as a structural basis, not measured physiologically here.

plain_language_summary: Hippocampal cells send long branches all over the brain, but those paths had not been drawn for thousands of single cells. This mouse study reconstructs more than ten thousand such cells and sorts them into projection types that depend on where the cell body sits.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM has reignited morphological description of complex tissue, while automated segmentation and 3D reconstruction pipelines now generate large quantitative datasets.
ocar.challenge: Users need practical guidance on sample preparation and analysis, and myelin biology is a demanding test case for membranes and pathology.
ocar.action: Schadt, Ruhwedel, Pape, Sasmita, Steyer, and Möbius review vEM sample-preparation and data-analysis strategies and show how the methods have advanced myelin biology and disease.
ocar.resolution: Automated segmentation yields quantitative readouts of cellular and organellar properties; open datasets let others ask new questions. The review also points to new instrumentation, methods, and software relevant beyond myelin.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a methods-and-application review; it invites use of open vEM datasets rather than presenting a new myelin connectome.

summaries.beginner: New three-dimensional electron-microscope methods can show how insulation around nerve fibers is built and how it fails in disease. This review explains how to prepare samples, how computers now help measure those pictures, and what has been learned about myelin.
summaries.intermediate: In Methods in Microscopy (2024), Schadt, Ruhwedel, Pape, Sasmita, Steyer, and Möbius review volume electron microscopy with a focus on myelin research. They discuss sample preparation and analysis pipelines, including automated segmentation for quantitative cellular and organellar readouts, and the value of open datasets. Applications to myelin biology and disease are showcased, alongside newer instrumentation, methods, and software that could transfer to other tissues.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/tutorial, not a primary reconstruction paper. Catalog stages include preparation, segmentation, and acquisition; method is volume EM. No new numeric myelin metrics are given in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: New three-dimensional electron-microscope methods can show how insulation around nerve fibers is built and how it fails in disease. This review explains how to prepare samples, how computers now help measure those pictures, and what has been learned about myelin.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain network analysis began in the 1980s with only a handful of connectomes and no human maps.
ocar.challenge: The field must now use a flood of individual and cross-species data rather than a few canonical matrices.
ocar.action: Kaiser reviews currently available structural connectivity, organizational principles, and common features across species, from C. elegans and fruit fly to pigeons, rodents, cats, non-human primates, and humans, noting efforts such as UK Biobank aiming at 100,000 human subjects.
ocar.resolution: Connectome data now exist for many species and, for some, many individuals, with shared organizational features. The review outlines current challenges and future work in making use of that information.
ocar.future_work: Kaiser explicitly flags outstanding challenges in using connectome information; those are the agenda rather than results.

summaries.beginner: Forty years ago scientists had almost no whole-brain wiring maps; now they have maps from worms, flies, birds, rodents, monkeys, and many people. This review surveys what those maps have in common and what is still hard to do with them.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2023), Kaiser reviews the shift from a handful of 1980s connectomes to large-scale databases. Non-invasive diffusion imaging and related methods now provide connectivity in many species and individuals; UK Biobank is cited as being on track to record structural and functional connectivity in 100,000 human subjects. The review covers available structural data, organizational principles, cross-species common features, and current challenges in using connectome information.
summaries.advanced: UK Biobank’s 100,000 figure is a stated trajectory, not a completed count in this paper. “Common features across species” are asserted at review level without a single meta-analytic table in the abstract. Catalog dataset is C. elegans; the review is multi-species including human MRI-scale connectomes.

plain_language_summary: Forty years ago scientists had almost no whole-brain wiring maps; now they have maps from worms, flies, birds, rodents, monkeys, and many people. This review surveys what those maps have in common and what is still hard to do with them.

ocar.opportunity: As biological connectomes become available, using them in algorithms often requires acyclic representations such as directed acyclic graphs.
ocar.challenge: Removing cycles can destroy biologically meaningful structure, so algorithms must be judged on how much authenticity they keep.
ocar.action: Li customizes depth-first search and minimum feedback arc set algorithms to remove cycles in the C. elegans adult hermaphrodite connectome and scores them on edges, sensory-to-neuromuscular-junction pathways, and other graph properties.
ocar.resolution: MFAS retains structural authenticity of the original graph significantly better than DFS on these metrics.
ocar.future_work: The evaluation is on one hermaphrodite connectome; whether MFAS remains preferable on larger, denser brains is not shown.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring maps contain loops, but some computer methods need a version without loops. This student-conference paper compares two ways of cutting loops and finds that one of them keeps the original shape of the map much better.
summaries.intermediate: At the 2023 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference, Benjamin Li customizes depth-first search (DFS) and minimum feedback arc set (MFAS) algorithms to remove cycles in the C. elegans adult hermaphrodite connectome. Performance is evaluated on edges, sensory-neuron-to-neuromuscular-junction pathways, and other graphical properties. MFAS retains structural authenticity of the original graph significantly better than DFS.
summaries.advanced: “Significantly better” is not accompanied by numeric scores in the abstract. Cycle removal is a modeling choice for DAG conversion, not a claim that the biological network is acyclic. Scope is the adult hermaphrodite chemical/electrical connectome as used by the author, not the male or other species.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring maps contain loops, but some computer methods need a version without loops. This student-conference paper compares two ways of cutting loops and finds that one of them keeps the original shape of the map much better.

ocar.opportunity: Retinal prostheses electrically stimulate surviving cells, but they are usually considered late, when mainly inner retina remains, and they still yield limited perception.
ocar.challenge: In early degeneration, bipolar cells still receive photoreceptor input, so their altered responses to electrical stimulation need to be understood separately for ON and OFF types.
ocar.action: Farzad, Kosta, Iseri, Jones, Lazzi, and colleagues build computational models of healthy and degenerated ON and OFF cone bipolar cells using realistic morphologies from healthy and early-stage degenerated rabbit-retina connectomes, varying pulse duration and electrode distance.
ocar.resolution: OFF CBCs show no significant membrane-potential difference between healthy and degenerate cells regardless of position. ON CBC axon-terminal membrane potential rises faster in healthy cells (time constant 0.29 ± 0.03 ms versus 0.8 ± 0.07 ms). Calcium current at axon terminals is higher in degenerated cells (32.24 ± 6.12 pA versus 13.64 ± 2.88 pA), independent of position.
ocar.future_work: The models address early-stage rabbit degeneration; translating stimulation parameters to human RP/AMD prostheses remains an extrapolation.

summaries.beginner: Eye implants try to electrically tickle remaining retinal cells after disease starts. This modeling study of rabbit retinas finds that one class of middle-layer cells responds differently when the retina is already degenerating, while another class looks similar, which could matter for how implants are programmed early in disease.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering (2023), Farzad, Kosta, Iseri, Walston, Bouteiller, Pfeiffer, Sigulinsky, Yang, Garcia, Anderson, Jones, and Lazzi model healthy and degenerated ON and OFF cone bipolar cells with morphologies from healthy and early-stage degenerated rabbit-retina connectomes. OFF CBC membrane potentials do not differ significantly with degeneration regardless of electrode position. Healthy ON CBC axon-terminal potentials rise with a shorter time constant (0.29 ± 0.03 ms vs 0.8 ± 0.07 ms). Axon-terminal calcium current is higher in degenerated cells (32.24 ± 6.12 pA vs 13.64 ± 2.88 pA), independent of position.
summaries.advanced: Results are computational, with morphologies from rabbit connectomes; catalog organism/dataset are tagged mouse retina (DS09/DS10), which does not match the rabbit morphologies named in the abstract—ground claims in the rabbit models. “No significant difference” for OFF cells is a model outcome. Calcium-current and time-constant values include reported means ± errors as in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Eye implants try to electrically tickle remaining retinal cells after disease starts. This modeling study of rabbit retinas finds that one class of middle-layer cells responds differently when the retina is already degenerating, while another class looks similar, which could matter for how implants are programmed early in disease.

ocar.opportunity: Insect vision has been probed by behavior and by physiology of motion and color, but form vision can now be read from a wiring diagram.
ocar.challenge: Which optic-lobe cell types could compute orientation, and how their connections map onto hypothesised cortical motifs, is not obvious from catalogs of names alone.
ocar.action: Seung interprets a Drosophila optic-lobe wiring diagram, analyzing Dm3 line amacrine cells and TmY cells, their facet-mapped inputs, and projections toward LC10 and form-learning regions.
ocar.resolution: Dm3 splits into three types with oriented dendrites, connected to three oriented TmY types, all predicted to be orientation-selective with preferred orientation set by dendrites. Dm3–Dm3 and Dm3–TmY connectivity approximates cross-orientation inhibition, and TmY–TmY approximates iso-orientation excitation—motifs previously hypothesized for mammalian visual cortex. Two TmY types target a novel LC10 type leading toward visual-form learning areas, and Seung conjectures flies may see illusory contours and corners.
ocar.future_work: Orientation selectivity, illusory contours, and corners are predictions and a conjecture from anatomy; they are not physiological confirmations in this abstract.

summaries.beginner: We know a lot about how flies see motion and color, but less about how they see shapes. By reading a wiring map of the fly eye’s brain, this paper predicts that some cells are tuned to lines of a particular tilt, using connection patterns similar to those proposed for mammalian visual cortex.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv preprint, H. S. Seung interprets a Drosophila optic-lobe wiring diagram for form vision. Dm3 line amacrine cells divide into three types with oriented dendrites and connect to three TmY types, also with oriented dendrites; all six are predicted to be orientation-selective from inputs that chiefly convey single-facet information. Dm3 connectivity approximates cross-orientation inhibition and TmY–TmY connectivity iso-orientation excitation, motifs previously hypothesized for mammalian visual cortex. Two TmY types target a novel LC10 type leading to visual-form learning regions, and Seung conjectures that flies may see illusory contours and corners.
summaries.advanced: All functional claims (orientation selectivity, illusory contours) are predictions or a conjecture from connectivity, not new recordings. Approximation to cortical motifs is analogical. Catalog organism is fly; stage graph analysis. The abstract does not name which EM volume is used.

plain_language_summary: We know a lot about how flies see motion and color, but less about how they see shapes. By reading a wiring map of the fly eye’s brain, this paper predicts that some cells are tuned to lines of a particular tilt, using connection patterns similar to those proposed for mammalian visual cortex.

ocar.opportunity: Topological data analysis of connectomes reports high Betti numbers, which might indicate interesting topology—or might be a byproduct of having many simplices.
ocar.challenge: Testing that requires a null model of directed graphs that keeps the undirected skeleton and similar simplex counts, and that can be sampled uniformly enough to be trusted.
ocar.action: Unger and Krebs introduce MCMC sampling of directed flag complexes with a fixed undirected graph, with a high-performance Rust implementation, and apply it to the C. elegans connectome and parts of Blue Brain Project statistical reconstructions.
ocar.resolution: Observed Betti numbers are considerable statistical outliers relative to this null model, statistically confirming that TDA in these microscale connectomes extracts meaningful information rather than a simplex-count artifact.
ocar.future_work: The null model holds the undirected graph fixed; other constraints (distance, cell type) would define different nulls still to be compared.

summaries.beginner: When scientists measure “holes” and loops in a wiring map, they need to know whether those shapes are special or just what you get from having many connections. This paper builds a fair random comparison and finds that worm and some simulated cortical maps really do look unusual.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Applied and Computational Topology (2023), Unger and Krebs provide a uniformly sampleable null model of directed graphs with similar flag-complex simplex counts while retaining the underlying undirected graph. An MCMC sampler, implemented in Rust, is applied to the C. elegans connectome and parts of Blue Brain Project statistical reconstructions. Betti numbers in the investigated graphs are considerable statistical outliers under this null, supporting that topological data analysis is extracting statistically meaningful information.
summaries.advanced: Mixing behavior of the MCMC is statistically investigated; the abstract does not quote mixing-time numbers. The Blue Brain application is to “parts of the statistical reconstructions,” not a full biologically acquired EM connectome. Outlier status is relative to this specific null (fixed undirected graph, similar simplex counts).

plain_language_summary: When scientists measure “holes” and loops in a wiring map, they need to know whether those shapes are special or just what you get from having many connections. This paper builds a fair random comparison and finds that worm and some simulated cortical maps really do look unusual.

ocar.opportunity: Network function depends not only on synapses but on neuromodulatory systems that broadcast via distributed connections and volume transmission.
ocar.challenge: The molecular constraints that organize neuromodulation in the adult zebrafish telencephalon had not been mapped at cell-type granularity.
ocar.action: Anneser, Satou, Hotz, and Friedrich use transcriptomics plus complementary approaches to delineate cell types, assess phylogenetic conservation, and map marker-gene expression, then examine combinatorial GPCR and cell-type-marker expression.
ocar.resolution: All neuronal cell types appear subject to multiple monoaminergic systems and distinct neuropeptide combinations. Types typically associate with many (typically >30) neuromodulatory networks but express only a few diagnostic GPCRs at high levels, suggesting unequal combined weights. The work yields a detailed map of telencephalic cell types and areas and core neuromodulatory components.
ocar.future_work: The logic of combinatorial neuromodulation is only begun to be deciphered; functional weights of the many low-level GPCRs remain to be measured.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells are influenced not only by fast point-to-point contacts but also by chemical broadcasts that reach many cells at once. This zebrafish study maps which cell types have the receivers for those chemicals and finds that every type can hear several systems, though usually only a few receivers are strong.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2023), Anneser, Satou, Hotz, and Friedrich map neuronal cell types and neuromodulatory systems in the adult zebrafish telencephalon with transcriptomics and high-granularity marker mapping. Combinatorial GPCR and cell-type-marker expression indicates every neuronal type is subject to multiple monoaminergic systems and distinct neuropeptide combinations. Individual types associate with typically more than 30 neuromodulatory signaling networks but express only a few diagnostic GPCRs at high levels. Results include phylogenetic conservation assessment and a map of cell types and brain areas.
summaries.advanced: “Typically >30” networks per type is the abstract’s figure; “all neuronal cell types” is a survey claim for the mapped telencephalon, not the whole fish. High-level diagnostic GPCRs versus many low-level associations is an expression-pattern inference, not a ranking of in vivo impact. Catalog dataset is DS15 zebrafish.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells are influenced not only by fast point-to-point contacts but also by chemical broadcasts that reach many cells at once. This zebrafish study maps which cell types have the receivers for those chemicals and finds that every type can hear several systems, though usually only a few receivers are strong.

ocar.opportunity: Female Drosophila change auditory behavior after hearing same-species courtship song, becoming less responsive to other species’ songs—an experience-dependent preference that requires GABAergic input to pC1 neurons.
ocar.challenge: The neurons that supply that GABA, and the circuit motifs that implement the learning, had not been identified.
ocar.action: Imoto, Ishikawa, Aso, Funke, Tanaka, and Kamikouchi combine RNAi, connectomics (including hemibrain), and circuit genetics around pC1 and pCd-2.
ocar.resolution: Four pCd-2 cells per hemibrain, doublesex-positive, provide the GABAergic input to pC1 needed for song-preference learning, connecting directly and often mutually with pC1. GABAergic and dopaminergic inputs to pCd-2 are also necessary. Reciprocal pC1–pCd-2 circuits are proposed as a sensory- and internal-state hub for flexible female copulation.
ocar.future_work: The paper offers a single-cell-resolution circuit model of auditory plasticity; how song statistics are stored in the dopaminergic/GABAergic inputs to pCd-2 is not fully specified in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Female fruit flies learn to prefer the courtship song of their own species after hearing it. This study finds a tiny set of inhibitory cells that talk back and forth with a known mating center, and that conversation is needed for the learning.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv preprint (also listed with an iScience-style identifier), Imoto, Ishikawa, Aso, Funke, Tanaka, and Kamikouchi identify pCd-2 neurons—four cells per hemibrain, expressing doublesex—as the GABAergic input to pC1 required for Drosophila song-preference learning. Knockdown of GABA production in pCd-2 abolishes learning. Connectomics shows direct, often mutual, pCd-2–pC1 connections. GABAergic and dopaminergic inputs to pCd-2 are necessary. The authors propose reciprocal pC1–pCd-2 circuits as an integrative hub for experience-dependent auditory control of copulation.
summaries.advanced: Necessity claims are from RNAi and input manipulations as stated; “often mutually” describes connectivity, not a measured oscillation. Catalog dataset is DS05 hemibrain. The abstract’s significance statement compares to other species’ auditory plasticity but the data are fly-specific.

plain_language_summary: Female fruit flies learn to prefer the courtship song of their own species after hearing it. This study finds a tiny set of inhibitory cells that talk back and forth with a known mating center, and that conversation is needed for the learning.

ocar.opportunity: Animals must tell externally caused sensory signals from those produced by their own movement, using predictive motor signals from motor pathways to sensory pathways.
ocar.challenge: How such corollary-discharge circuits work at cellular and synaptic resolution is poorly understood.
ocar.action: Cheong, Boone, Bennett, Lee, Card, Daly, Dacks, and colleagues use male and female EM connectomes, transcriptomics, anatomy, physiology, and behavior to resolve two pairs of ascending histaminergic neurons (AHNs).
ocar.resolution: Both AHN pairs receive input mainly from an overlapping set of descending neurons, many of which drive wing motor output. The two pairs target almost exclusively non-overlapping downstream networks for visual, auditory, and mechanosensory processing and for wing, haltere, and leg motor coordination. AHNs thus multi-task: they integrate common motor-related input and tile predictive signals across distinct sensory-motor networks.
ocar.future_work: The abstract supports a putatively predictive role; causal tests that AHN activity is necessary to cancel reafference in each sensory modality are only partly implied by the combined methods list.

summaries.beginner: When an animal moves, its sensors fire because of that movement, not only because the world changed. This fly study maps two pairs of upward-going cells that collect motor commands and send copies into different sensory and motor areas, a possible way to predict self-made sensations.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv preprint, Cheong, Boone, Bennett, Salman, Ralston, Hatch, Allen, Phelps, Cook, Phelps, Erginkaya, Lee, Card, Daly, and Dacks analyze two pairs of ascending histaminergic neurons with connectomics from male and female EM volumes plus transcriptomics, physiology, and behavior. Both pairs receive primarily overlapping descending-neuron input, much of it wing-related. Their outputs tile almost non-overlapping visual, auditory, mechanosensory, and wing/haltere/leg motor networks. The authors conclude that AHNs integrate common input then provide predictive motor signals to distinct sensory networks, affecting motor control directly and indirectly.
summaries.advanced: “Putatively provide predictive motor signals” is the authors’ framing. Male and female volumes are both used; the abstract does not detail sexual dimorphism of AHNs. Catalog lists no organism; methods include electron microscopy; the system is insect flight-related (wing, haltere).

plain_language_summary: When an animal moves, its sensors fire because of that movement, not only because the world changed. This fly study maps two pairs of upward-going cells that collect motor commands and send copies into different sensory and motor areas, a possible way to predict self-made sensations.

ocar.opportunity: A single cue such as sugar can drive feeding, change locomotion to find food, and assign reward to contexts—multiple appetitive behaviors from one sensory quality.
ocar.challenge: Whether those behaviors are coordinately regulated, and where the sugar circuit diverges, was unknown in Drosophila.
ocar.action: Jacobs, Wang, Nguyen, Devineni, and colleagues establish an optogenetic paradigm for locomotion, spatial preference, and associative learning, then manipulate hunger, diet, aversive taste, and each layer of a previously described five-layer feeding-initiation circuit, with connectomic analyses of subcircuits.
ocar.resolution: Different sugar-evoked behaviors are generally modulated similarly, with some selective pathway modulation. Circuits for different innate responses overlap and begin to diverge at second- and third-order neurons, whereas innate versus learned circuits may diverge at the first synapse. Distinct connectomic subcircuits map onto different behaviors.
ocar.future_work: The first-synapse split for learned versus innate behavior is a “may” in the abstract; finer causal dissection of each subcircuit remains open.

summaries.beginner: Sweet taste makes an animal eat, hunt for food, and remember places associated with sugar. This fruit-fly study asks whether those actions share the same nerve cells and finds that the paths start together and then split, with learning possibly splitting off even earlier.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv preprint, Jacobs, Wang, Nguyen, Pruitt, Wang, Lozada-Perdomo, Deere, Liphart, and Devineni study how Drosophila sugar taste drives multiple appetitive behaviors. An optogenetic paradigm probes locomotion, spatial preference, and associative learning. Hunger, diet, and aversive taste generally modulate these behaviors similarly, with some differences indicating selective pathway modulation. Manipulating neurons of a five-layer feeding-initiation circuit shows partial overlap of innate-response circuits, divergence at second- and third-order neurons, and possible divergence of innate versus learned circuits at the first synapse. Connectomics reveals distinct behavioral subcircuits.
summaries.advanced: Coordinate versus selective modulation is described as “generally similar” with some differences; the abstract does not list which behavior was the exception. The five-layer feeding circuit is from a cited recent study, not re-derived here. Innate-versus-learned first-synapse divergence is hedged with “may.”

plain_language_summary: Sweet taste makes an animal eat, hunt for food, and remember places associated with sugar. This fruit-fly study asks whether those actions share the same nerve cells and finds that the paths start together and then split, with learning possibly splitting off even earlier.

ocar.opportunity: Self-organized criticality is thought to be a fundamental property for normal function, often read out as avalanches in large networks.
ocar.challenge: Avalanche statistics are ill-suited to small networks such as C. elegans, whose 302 neurons may not support avalanche emergence, so another signature is needed.
ocar.action: Gu, Liu, Yuan, Zhao, Xin, and Fang build a directed-graph model from the C. elegans connectome, simulate gradient potentials and activity, and use the branching parameter, then compare to experimental calcium activity.
ocar.resolution: Branching-parameter analysis is reported to prove self-organized criticality in the worm network, with further confirmation from calcium-activity data.
ocar.future_work: The result is for this 302-neuron model plus calcium recordings; whether branching-parameter criticality is necessary for particular behaviors is not addressed in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Large brain networks sometimes sit at a special balance point between quiet and runaway activity. This paper asks whether the tiny worm nervous system sits at a similar balance, using a wiring-based simulation and calcium recordings rather than the avalanche method used in bigger brains.
summaries.intermediate: At a 2023 Cybersecurity and Cyberforensics Conference venue listing, Gu, Liu, Yuan, Zhao, Xin, and Fang argue that avalanche-based tests of self-organized criticality do not fit the 302-neuron C. elegans network. They construct a directed-graph model from the connectome, simulate neuronal gradient potentials and activity, and use the branching parameter to describe activity propagation. They report that this analysis proves SOC in the worm network and confirm the result with experimentally obtained calcium activity.
summaries.advanced: “Proved” is the authors’ wording; the abstract does not give the branching-parameter value or a statistical test. Conference venue metadata in the catalog may not match a neuroscience-typical outlet. Calcium confirmation is mentioned without recording counts or conditions.

plain_language_summary: Large brain networks sometimes sit at a special balance point between quiet and runaway activity. This paper asks whether the tiny worm nervous system sits at a similar balance, using a wiring-based simulation and calcium recordings rather than the avalanche method used in bigger brains.

ocar.opportunity: Animals must convert an object’s location on the retina into a movement direction in the body, a visuomotor transform that remains largely unknown at circuit resolution.
ocar.challenge: How topographic visual maps become directed motor output is hard to see without combining behavior, physiology, anatomy, and connectomics.
ocar.action: Dombrovski, Peek, Park, Card, Zipursky, and colleagues study Drosophila looming, focusing on visual projection neurons and two postsynaptic neurons that promote opposite takeoff directions.
ocar.resolution: Feature-detecting VPN dendritic maps are converted into synaptic-weight gradients onto central neurons, often without VPN axon topography. Opposite weight gradients from looming VPNs in different visual-field regions orient escape, and a second VPN type shows graded dorsoventral responses. The synaptic-gradient motif generalizes across all 20 primary VPN types.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose synaptic gradients as a general mechanism from spatial sensory features to directed motor output; tests beyond looming and beyond these 20 VPN types are outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: To dodge something coming from the left, an animal must turn its view of “left” into a body movement to the correct side. In fruit flies, this study shows that the strength of connections, laid out as a smooth gradient, can turn a location on the eye into an escape in the right direction.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2023), Dombrovski, Peek, Park, Vaccari, Sumathipala, Morrow, Breads, Zhao, Kurmangaliyev, Sanfilippo, Rehan, Polsky, Alghailani, Tenshaw, Namiki, Zipursky, and Card show that Drosophila visuomotor transformation converts topographic dendritic maps of feature-detecting visual projection neurons into synaptic-weight gradients onto central brain neurons. Two neurons postsynaptic to a looming-responsive VPN type promote opposite takeoff directions; opposite synaptic-weight gradients from VPNs in different visual-field regions produce correctly oriented escapes. A second looming VPN type has graded dorsoventral responses. The motif generalizes across all 20 primary VPN types and most often arises without VPN axon topography.
summaries.advanced: Generalization “across all 20 primary VPN cell types” is the authors’ connectomic claim; functional tests in the abstract center on looming escape. Catalog dataset is listed as mouse retina, which conflicts with the Drosophila subject—ground the science in the fly data. “Most often arises without VPN axon topography” is an important caveat for assuming spatial maps live in axons.

plain_language_summary: To dodge something coming from the left, an animal must turn its view of “left” into a body movement to the correct side. In fruit flies, this study shows that the strength of connections, laid out as a smooth gradient, can turn a location on the eye into an escape in the right direction.

ocar.opportunity: Neurological disease burden is rising, and Big Data has begun to transform neuroscience and neurology through global alliances, massive combined datasets, and heavy computation.
ocar.challenge: The potential of Big Data for patient care is still unrealized, with technical limits that differ by disease area.
ocar.action: Dipietro, Gonzalez-Mego, Ramos-Estebanez, Wagner, and colleagues survey Big Data in connectomics, Alzheimer disease, stroke, depression, Parkinson’s disease, pain, and addiction including opioid use disorder.
ocar.resolution: They review methods and limitations in each area and close with recommendations to optimize Big Data use for patient outcomes.
ocar.future_work: The recommendations are the forward-looking content; the paper is a survey, not a new clinical trial.

summaries.beginner: Brain diseases are common, and researchers now work with very large shared datasets and computers. This survey asks how that “big data” turn has helped areas such as stroke, Alzheimer disease, and addiction, and why the benefits for patients are still limited.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Big Data (2023), Dipietro, Gonzalez-Mego, Ramos-Estebanez, Zukowski, Mikkilineni, Rushmore, and Wagner survey Big Data’s impact on neurological care across connectomics, Alzheimer disease, stroke, depression, Parkinson’s disease, pain, and addiction (e.g., opioid use disorder). They review methodologies, current limitations, and technical challenges in each area, arguing that the full potential remains unrealized, and they offer recommendations for future research aimed at improved patient outcomes.
summaries.advanced: This is a broad survey, not a systematic review with inclusion counts in the abstract. “Unrealized potential” is the authors’ assessment. Catalog dimension is review; no organism or method tags.

plain_language_summary: Brain diseases are common, and researchers now work with very large shared datasets and computers. This survey asks how that “big data” turn has helped areas such as stroke, Alzheimer disease, and addiction, and why the benefits for patients are still limited.

ocar.opportunity: Complete single-neuron reconstructions now make previously inaccessible thalamocortical connectivity patterns analyzable, which is key to how thalamus relays sensory input to cortex.
ocar.challenge: Linking topography, higher-order projection combinations, and morphological diversity in a single workflow is still difficult.
ocar.action: Timonidis, Bakker, Clascá, Tiesinga, and colleagues analyze 257 ventral posteromedial (VPM) neurons from MouseLight and Braintell, cluster them by dominant cortical targets, embed axonal morphology, and release a portal with cortical flatmap visualization.
ocar.resolution: A curved 2D morphological embedding reduces to a 1-D coordinate aligned with soma position along dorsal–ventral and lateral–medial axes, axonal terminals along posterior–anterior and medial–lateral axes, and increases in branch points, soma distance, and branching width. The workflow ties topography, higher-order targets, and morphology for VPM as a test case.
ocar.future_work: Processed data are released in Python for modeling and experimental validation of new thalamocortical hypotheses; those validations are invited, not completed here.

summaries.beginner: Thalamic cells carry touch information up to the cortex, but each cell’s long branches look different. This mouse study sorts hundreds of fully traced cells by where they go and by shape, and puts the results in a shared website for others to use.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2023), Timonidis, Bakker, Rubio-Teves, Alonso-Martínez, García-Amado, Clascá, and Tiesinga characterize 257 mouse VPM neurons from MouseLight and Braintell. Neurons are clustered by most dominant cortical target and subdivided by jointly targeted areas. A 2D embedding of axonal-tree dissimilarities has a curved shape that they reduce to a 1-D coordinate aligned with soma position (dorsal–ventral, lateral–medial), terminal fields (posterior–anterior, medial–lateral), and morphological complexity. A portal integrates morphologies with 2D cortical flatmap and subcortical viewers.
summaries.advanced: n = 257 combined across two public projects; sampling biases of those projects are not discussed in the abstract. The 1-D coordinate is a description of the embedding’s alignment, not a proven developmental axis. Catalog stages include preparation and graph analysis; organism mouse.

plain_language_summary: Thalamic cells carry touch information up to the cortex, but each cell’s long branches look different. This mouse study sorts hundreds of fully traced cells by where they go and by shape, and puts the results in a shared website for others to use.

ocar.opportunity: Sexual dimorphism in nervous systems has often been attributed to sex-specific neurons, but sex-shared neurons can also generate sex differences.
ocar.challenge: The anatomical and functional ways shared cells differ—and the molecules that build those differences—need a systematic account in a connectome-complete animal.
ocar.action: Kim and Kim review anatomical and functional differences in C. elegans sex-shared neurons.
ocar.resolution: Dimorphisms include neurite projection or branching changes with substantial synaptic rewiring, synaptic differences without obvious structural change, and functional modulation with little or no connectivity change. The review covers molecular mechanisms that establish dimorphic circuits in development and that make shared neurons function differently in adults.
ocar.future_work: As a review, it organizes known mechanisms rather than reporting a new whole-animal dimorphic connectome.

summaries.beginner: Males and females can behave differently even when they share the same named nerve cells. This review of the worm C. elegans explains that those shared cells can grow extra branches, change their contacts, or simply run differently without a visible wiring change.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2022), Dongyoung Kim and Byunghyuk Kim review sex-shared neurons in C. elegans. They catalog morphological differences in neurite projection or branching with substantial synaptic-connectivity change, synaptic differences without obvious structure change, and functional modulation with no or minimal connectivity change. They also review molecular mechanisms that build dimorphic circuits during development and that make shared neurons function differently between sexes.
summaries.advanced: This is a review centered on sex-shared cells, complementary to work on sex-specific neurons. No new synapse counts appear in the abstract. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans.

plain_language_summary: Males and females can behave differently even when they share the same named nerve cells. This review of the worm C. elegans explains that those shared cells can grow extra branches, change their contacts, or simply run differently without a visible wiring change.

ocar.opportunity: SEM acquisition is too slow for large volumes on feasible timescales; low-dose sparse imaging plus computational reconstruction is one way forward.
ocar.challenge: Denoising and inpainting at acceptable quality need significant compute, which can block live or delayed-live reconstruction during acquisition.
ocar.action: Putter, Peemen, Potocek, Schoenmakers, and Corporaal propose CELR: local CNN reconstruction that approximates a classical algorithm (GOAL), with recurring CNN training and GOAL label generation in the cloud, plus TensorRT throughput optimization.
ocar.resolution: CELR plus TensorRT enables large-volume acquisitions with 1 μs dwell time and 10% pixel coverage to be reconstructed on a single GPU. The paper also discusses open questions about on-the-fly CNN training.
ocar.future_work: On-the-fly training remains an open research question the authors explicitly flag.

summaries.beginner: Taking a complete electron-microscope picture of a large sample can be painfully slow. This work sketches a split system: a fast local computer fills in missing pixels while a remote computer keeps teaching it, so imaging can stay sparse and still look usable.
summaries.intermediate: At the 2022 Euromicro Symposium on Digital Systems Design, Putter, Peemen, Potocek, Schoenmakers, and Corporaal present CELR (Cloud Enhanced Local Reconstruction) for low-dose sparse SEM. Local CNNs approximate a classical reconstructor (GOAL) for delayed-live reconstruction, while CNN retraining and GOAL label generation run in the cloud. TensorRT is used to optimize CNN throughput. Combined, large-volume acquisitions with 1 μs dwell time and 10% pixel coverage can be reconstructed on a single GPU.
summaries.advanced: The 1 μs / 10% / single-GPU claim is the headline capability; image-quality metrics versus fully sampled SEM are not in the abstract. CNNs approximate GOAL rather than claiming a new gold-standard reconstructor. On-the-fly training is listed as open. Catalog method is SEM; stages acquisition and infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Taking a complete electron-microscope picture of a large sample can be painfully slow. This work sketches a split system: a fast local computer fills in missing pixels while a remote computer keeps teaching it, so imaging can stay sparse and still look usable.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila olfactory projection neurons are transcriptionally diverse; whether that diversity shows up as bouton ultrastructure was unknown.
ocar.challenge: Quantifying internal presynaptic active zones and dense-core vesicles requires volumetric EM reconstruction of many boutons.
ocar.action: Yang, Liu, Wang, Guo, Han, Di, Zhang, and colleagues volumetrically reconstruct 89 PN boutons with FIB-SEM and cluster them by PAZ and DCV ultrastructure, including a labeled GH146-positive subset.
ocar.resolution: Three morphological subtypes appear: complex, unilobed, and simple. Complex boutons contain the most PAZs and DCVs, suggesting the highest capacity to release neurotransmitters and neuromodulators. DCVs are preferentially distributed in certain GH146-positive subtypes.
ocar.future_work: The 89-bouton sample and GH146 subset do not assign every PN type to a bouton class; linking clusters to full transcriptomic types remains open.

summaries.beginner: Smell-carrying cells in the fruit fly look molecularly diverse, but it was unclear whether their ending swellings look different too. By reconstructing 89 swellings in three-dimensional electron-microscope data, this study finds three shapes, with the most complex ones packed with the machinery to release chemical messengers.
summaries.intermediate: In iScience (2022), Yang, Liu, Wang, Liu, Shen, Pan, Wen, Xie, Ruan, Tan, Chen, Guo, Liu, Han, Di, and Zhang reconstruct 89 Drosophila olfactory projection-neuron boutons with FIB-SEM and quantify presynaptic active zones and dense-core vesicles. Ultrastructure-based clustering yields complex, unilobed, and simple boutons. Complex boutons have the most PAZs and DCVs, interpreted as highest release capacity for transmitters and neuromodulators. In a labeled subset, DCVs are preferentially distributed in certain GH146-positive subtypes.
summaries.advanced: n = 89 boutons; clustering is ultrastructure-based, not a complete PN-type census. “Highest capability” of complex boutons is an inference from PAZ/DCV counts, not a physiological release assay. Catalog method is FIB-SEM; stages include sectioning and acquisition.

plain_language_summary: Smell-carrying cells in the fruit fly look molecularly diverse, but it was unclear whether their ending swellings look different too. By reconstructing 89 swellings in three-dimensional electron-microscope data, this study finds three shapes, with the most complex ones packed with the machinery to release chemical messengers.

ocar.opportunity: Reservoir computing maps inputs through a high-dimensional recurrent network, usually with a static random topology, and it is unclear how that topology affects learning.
ocar.challenge: Simple random-graph descriptions may miss the complex features of real connectomes that could matter for performance.
ocar.action: d'Andrea, Puppin, Kessler, and colleagues test synthetic networks with varied topology and 45 empirical connectomes from brain regions of eight species on a prediction task with diverse input signals.
ocar.resolution: Performance correlates nontrivially with node number and with the rank of the covariance of activation states, depending on whether inputs are stochastic or deterministic. Modularity and link density affect performance in ways not predicted by models that only keep simple topological features. Complex connectome-like features can thus inform bio-inspired reservoir design.
ocar.future_work: The result is for a prediction-task battery; other RC tasks and training readouts might weight topological features differently.

summaries.beginner: Some artificial networks keep a fixed inner tangle of connections and only train a simple readout. This study asks whether using real brain-like tangles, not just random ones, changes how well those systems predict incoming signals, and finds that community structure and connection density matter.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 paper (journal field empty in the catalog), d'Andrea, Puppin, Kessler and colleagues study how reservoir topology shapes reservoir-computing performance. They use synthetic networks with different topological features and 45 empirical connectomes from brain regions of eight species, on a prediction task with varied complex inputs. They find nontrivial correlations of performance with node count and with the rank of the activation-state covariance matrix, with effects depending on stochastic versus deterministic inputs. Modularity and link density affect performance beyond what simple topological models predict.
summaries.advanced: The catalog record has an empty journal string and messy author-address fields; treat bibliographic venue as uncertain. “45 empirical connectomes… 8 species” is the sample as stated; species list is not in the abstract. Performance dependence on input class is a caveat against one-topology-fits-all design.

plain_language_summary: Some artificial networks keep a fixed inner tangle of connections and only train a simple readout. This study asks whether using real brain-like tangles, not just random ones, changes how well those systems predict incoming signals, and finds that community structure and connection density matter.

ocar.opportunity: Papilio xuthus has six spectral photoreceptor classes, three ommatidial types, and 1 nm wavelength discrimination from UV to red, far beyond Drosophila’s limited color vision.
ocar.challenge: The neuronal basis of that precision, and how such systems evolve, requires comparative circuit-level data starting at the first optic ganglion.
ocar.action: Matsushita, Stewart, Arikawa, and colleagues perform a lamina connectome analysis of P. xuthus, describing cartridges that typically contain nine photoreceptor axons and four second-order neurons.
ocar.resolution: They find abundant inter-photoreceptor connections absent in the D. melanogaster lamina, plus connections between neighboring cartridges, especially those from spectrally distinct ommatidia. Linear summation of synaptic connections well explains spectral sensitivities of photoreceptors and second-order lamina neurons.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a lamina connectome; deeper ganglia that may finish wavelength discrimination are not mapped here.

summaries.beginner: Swallowtail butterflies see color in extremely fine steps, much finer than fruit flies. By mapping the first relay of the butterfly eye, this study finds extra connections among light sensors themselves that flies lack, and those connections help explain how color sensitivity is shaped so early.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), Matsushita, Stewart, Ilić, Chen, Wakita, Miyazaki, Murata, Kinoshita, Belušič, and Arikawa report a lamina connectome of Papilio xuthus. Cartridges typically contain nine photoreceptor axons from one ommatidium and four second-order neurons. Unlike Drosophila, the butterfly lamina has abundant inter-photoreceptor connections and inter-cartridge links, especially among spectrally distinct ommatidia. Linear summation of synaptic connections well explains spectral sensitivity of photoreceptors and second-order neurons. The work is framed as comparative circuit analysis of precise color vision.
summaries.advanced: “Well explains” spectral sensitivity is a linear-summation account, not a full behavior-to-circuit model of 1 nm discrimination. Catalog organism is tagged fly; the species is butterfly (Papilio). Comparison to Drosophila lamina (no inter-photoreceptor connections) is central. Deeper optic ganglia are out of scope.

plain_language_summary: Swallowtail butterflies see color in extremely fine steps, much finer than fruit flies. By mapping the first relay of the butterfly eye, this study finds extra connections among light sensors themselves that flies lack, and those connections help explain how color sensitivity is shaped so early.

ocar.opportunity: 3D electron microscopy is central to cell biology, but identifying intracellular structures by hand is laborious and limits use of large volumes.
ocar.challenge: Structures span a wide range of size and complexity, and models trained in one imaging condition often fail in another.
ocar.action: Gallusser, Maltese, Weigert, Kirchhausen, and colleagues introduce ASEM, training a convolutional network per structure from a small number of sparse annotations in one or two cells, with a rapid refinement strategy when imaging conditions change.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate automatic identification of mitochondria, Golgi, ER, nuclear pore complexes, clathrin-coated pits and vesicles, and caveolae in quasi-isotropic FIB-SEM. Dedicated models come from sparse labels in only one or two cells.
ocar.future_work: The pipeline is shown on a defined organelle set in FIB-SEM; expanding classes and cross-lab imaging conditions still depends on the refinement protocol.

summaries.beginner: Cell biologists using three-dimensional electron microscopes spend huge amounts of time outlining organelles by hand. This method trains a computer on a few sparsely labeled examples from one or two cells and then finds those organelles automatically, with a shortcut to retune when the pictures look different.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 bioRxiv preprint (also associated with Journal of Cell Biology in the DOI), Gallusser, Maltese, Di Caprio, Vadakkan, Sanyal, Somerville, Sahasrabudhe, O'Connor, Weigert, and Kirchhausen present ASEM (Automated Segmentation of intracellular substructures in Electron Microscopy). Each structure gets a dedicated convolutional model trained on sparse annotations from one or two cells. A computationally light refinement adds a few annotations to adapt to new imaging conditions. Demonstrations on FIB-SEM include mitochondria, Golgi, ER, nuclear pores, clathrin-coated pits and vesicles, and caveolae.
summaries.advanced: Success is reported for the listed organelles at quasi-isotropic FIB-SEM resolution; the abstract does not give Dice scores. “One or two cells” of sparse ground truth is a data-efficiency claim that still requires expert annotation of those cells. Refinement is proposed as the generalization mechanism rather than a single universal model.

plain_language_summary: Cell biologists using three-dimensional electron microscopes spend huge amounts of time outlining organelles by hand. This method trains a computer on a few sparsely labeled examples from one or two cells and then finds those organelles automatically, with a shortcut to retune when the pictures look different.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila visual behaviors can now be dissected with genetics, tethered and freely moving assays, physiology, and connectomics.
ocar.challenge: The path from photons to behavior is split across many feature channels—brightness, color, local motion, optic flow, translating or approaching objects—and it is easy to lose an integrative picture.
ocar.action: Ryu, Kim, and Kim review how the fly visual system detects those features and how circuits turn them into phototaxis, optomotor responses, attraction or aversion to moving objects, navigation, and visual learning.
ocar.resolution: The review offers an integrative framework for how the fly brain detects visual features and orchestrates appropriate behavior.
ocar.future_work: As a review, it organizes recent circuit work rather than presenting a new reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies see the world well enough to steer, land, and learn visual patterns. This review walks through how different visual features are detected in the fly brain and turned into actions.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2022), Ryu, Kim, and Kim review neural implementations of Drosophila visual behaviors. They cover detection of brightness, color, local motion, optic flow, and translating or approaching objects, and the behaviors those features support: phototaxis, optomotor response, attraction or aversion to moving objects, navigation, and visual learning. Genetic toolkits, tethered and freely moving assays, and connectomics are the enabling context. The review aims at an integrative photons-to-behavior framework.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a primary connectome. Catalog stage is infrastructure; organism fly. No new numeric results appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies see the world well enough to steer, land, and learn visual patterns. This review walks through how different visual features are detected in the fly brain and turned into actions.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome research has grown into a large literature that is hard to see as a whole.
ocar.challenge: Identifying productive journals, countries, institutions, and topic shifts needs both bibliometrics and a topic model, not citation anecdotes.
ocar.action: Yan, Fan, Liao, and Zhao retrieve 14,140 publications from Web of Science and Scopus (2005–2021), compare journals, countries, and institutions, and apply latent Dirichlet allocation plus bibliometrix analyses.
ocar.resolution: NEUROIMAGE led in volume (1,427 articles) and h-index (122); most articles came from developed countries, especially the United States, with Harvard Medical School and the University of Pennsylvania the two most productive institutions. Major topics split into neuroimaging-analysis technology versus brain functions and diseases. Trends include machine learning, deep learning, graph theory, and dynamic functional connectivity, with recent foci on alcohol-use disorders and migraine.
ocar.future_work: The window ends in 2021; EM-scale invertebrate connectomes may be under-weighted relative to MRI-scale human work in these databases.

summaries.beginner: So many papers now use the word “connectome” that it is hard to see who writes them and what they are about. This study counts more than fourteen thousand papers and finds that imaging methods and brain diseases dominate, with machine learning a rising theme.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2022), Yan, Fan, Liao, and Zhao bibliometrically analyze 14,140 connectome publications from WoSCC and Scopus (2005–2021). NEUROIMAGE ranked first by volume (1,427 articles) and h-index (122). Output was concentrated in developed countries, led by the United States; Harvard Medical School and the University of Pennsylvania were the most productive institutions. LDA separated neuroimaging-analysis technology from brain functions and diseases. Reported trends include machine learning, deep learning, graph theory, and dynamic functional connectivity, with recent attention to alcohol-use disorders and migraine.
summaries.advanced: Counts depend on database coverage and the query that defined “connectomes.” h-index 122 is for the journal in this retrieved set as reported. Catalog stages include infrastructure and graph analysis; this paper is bibliometrics, not a biological network result. The 2005–2021 window misses later whole-brain EM maps.

plain_language_summary: So many papers now use the word “connectome” that it is hard to see who writes them and what they are about. This study counts more than fourteen thousand papers and finds that imaging methods and brain diseases dominate, with machine learning a rising theme.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding how living brain networks are structured, compute, and change needs comprehensive visualization of architecture with cellular and molecular context over time.
ocar.challenge: EM gives nanometer reconstruction but only of fixed, static tissue; super-resolution light microscopy can be live but has been blocked from saturated 3D reconstruction by photoburden, bleaching, insufficient 3D resolution, and poor SNR.
ocar.action: Velicky, Miguel, Michalska, Danzl, and colleagues adapt STED microscopy in extracellularly labeled tissue for high SNR and isotropic resolution, plus a two-stage deep-learning approach that uses prior structural information to cut photoburden and automate reconstruction to synapses.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate saturated reconstruction of living brain tissue, enabling unbiased analysis of architecture over time in relation to activity and targeted activation, and contextual molecular labeling.
ocar.future_work: The technology is presented as adoptable for dynamic functional architecture; long-term phototoxicity limits and brain-region coverage are not quantified in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can draw every tiny contact in dead tissue, while light microscopes can watch living tissue but not usually at that completeness. This paper combines a super-resolution light method with machine learning to reconstruct living brain tissue down to the level of contacts, so structure can be watched as it changes.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 bioRxiv preprint, Velicky, Miguel, Michalska, Wei, Lin, Watson, Troidl, Beyer, Ben-Simon, Sommer, Jahr, Cenameri, Broichhagen, Grant, Jonas, Novarino, Pfister, Bickel, and Danzl report saturated reconstruction of living brain tissue. They adapt STED microscopy with extracellular labeling for high SNR and isotropic resolution, and use a two-stage deep-learning approach that leverages prior sample-structure information to reduce photoburden and automate volumetric reconstruction to synapse level. Live reconstruction is aimed at relating architecture to functional activity and molecular labels over time.
summaries.advanced: “Saturated” is the authors’ term for comprehensive live reconstruction to synapses; completeness metrics are not in the abstract. Catalog dataset is DS11 Kasthuri neocortex and organism mouse—the abstract does not name Kasthuri; ground the method in STED of living, extracellularly labeled tissue. Comparison to EM is conceptual (live versus fixed), not a paired dual-modality volume in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can draw every tiny contact in dead tissue, while light microscopes can watch living tissue but not usually at that completeness. This paper combines a super-resolution light method with machine learning to reconstruct living brain tissue down to the level of contacts, so structure can be watched as it changes.

ocar.opportunity: How circuits self-assemble from neuronal stem cells is a core developmental question, especially how different lineages wire a specific motif.
ocar.challenge: Lineage, birth timing, and connectivity are rarely measured together with physiology and network science in the same circuit.
ocar.action: Wang, Wreden, Levy, Marshall, MacLean, and Heckscher combine Twin-spot MARCM, Multi-color Flip Out, permanent labeling, calcium imaging, connectomics, and network analyses in the Drosophila larval nerve cord.
ocar.resolution: Many lineages form temporal cohorts with sharp transitions in input connectivity, and a feed-forward motif encoding vibration-stimulus onset is assembled by preferential connectivity between temporal cohorts of different lineages. Connectivity does not follow an early-to-early, late-to-late rule; output neurons are born before input neurons (sequential addition). New genetic tools are generated for the community.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest sequential addition (outputs oldest, inputs youngest) could be a general strategy for feed-forward circuits, a comparative hypothesis.

summaries.beginner: Nerve cells are born in waves from stem cells, and it is not obvious how those waves become a working circuit. In the fruit-fly larva, this study finds a chain of cells that detects the start of a vibration is built by adding younger input cells onto older output cells, not the other way around.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 bioRxiv preprint, Wang, Wreden, Levy, Marshall, MacLean, and Heckscher study how Drosophila larval nerve-cord lineages assemble a feed-forward circuit. Developmental genetics (Twin-spot MARCM, Multi-color Flip Out, permanent labeling) are combined with calcium imaging, connectomics, and network science. Temporal cohorts—lineage-related neurons born in a tight window—show sharp transitions in input connectivity. A feed-forward motif encoding vibration-onset is built by preferential inter-lineage cohort connectivity, with output neurons born before input neurons rather than early-to-early/late-to-late matching.
summaries.advanced: The early-to-early, late-to-late model is explicitly rejected for this motif. Generalization to other feed-forward circuits is suggested, not shown. Catalog dataset is DS03 Drosophila larva. “Many lineages” is qualitative.

plain_language_summary: Nerve cells are born in waves from stem cells, and it is not obvious how those waves become a working circuit. In the fruit-fly larva, this study finds a chain of cells that detects the start of a vibration is built by adding younger input cells onto older output cells, not the other way around.

ocar.opportunity: Deeper layers of auditory systems have not been fully mapped in any model system.
ocar.challenge: Without a dispatch-style synthesis, new connectomic-plus-physiology papers on fly song circuits can be hard to place for a broad audience.
ocar.action: Bates and Jefferis highlight a study that links comprehensive Drosophila song-perception connectomics to physiological response profiles.
ocar.resolution: The preview frames that work as synaptic-resolution auditory systems neuroscience.
ocar.future_work: As a Current Biology dispatch, it points to the highlighted paper rather than adding new data.

summaries.beginner: How brains hear courtship song at the level of every contact is still being mapped. This short piece introduces a fruit-fly study that ties a detailed wiring diagram of song circuits to how those cells actually fire.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), Bates and Jefferis preview progress on auditory processing at synaptic resolution. They note that deeper layers of the auditory system have not been fully mapped in any model system. The dispatch highlights a new study that links comprehensive connectomics of Drosophila song-perception circuits to physiological response profiles, placing that work as systems neuroscience at synaptic resolution.
summaries.advanced: This is a dispatch/preview, not a primary methods or data paper. Claims about mapping completeness refer to the field and the highlighted study. Catalog organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: How brains hear courtship song at the level of every contact is still being mapped. This short piece introduces a fruit-fly study that ties a detailed wiring diagram of song circuits to how those cells actually fire.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping dense cellular arrangement and connectivity in brain tissue demands nanoscale resolution, but super-resolution light microscopy usually lacks tissue context.
ocar.challenge: Seeing identified synapses and regional architecture together, in chemically fixed rodent and human tissue, requires a labeling and readout strategy that is fixation-compatible and dense.
ocar.action: Michalska, Lyudchik, Velicky, Danzl, and colleagues develop CATS (Comprehensive Analysis of Tissues across Scales), using extracellular labeling plus STED and expansion microscopy to delineate cellular structures from millimeter to synaptic scales.
ocar.resolution: CATS enables 3D reconstruction of single synapses and mapping of synaptic connectivity via analysis of putative synaptic clefts. Applied to hippocampal mossy-fiber circuitry, it reveals molecularly informed ultrastructure across scales and local connectivity of identified neurons’ synaptic input and output.
ocar.future_work: Putative cleft identification is tailored analysis, not EM-proof of every synapse; applying CATS as a routine human-pathology pipeline is a stated capability, not a clinical study here.

summaries.beginner: Super-resolution light microscopes can see labeled molecules but often miss the dense packing of all the cells around them. This method stains the spaces between cells so that many cell outlines, and likely contact zones, can be mapped from large regions down to synapses in rodent and human brain tissue.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 bioRxiv preprint, Michalska, Lyudchik, Velicky, Korinkova, Watson, Cenameri, Sommer, Venturino, Roessler, Czech, Siegert, Novarino, Jonas, and Danzl introduce CATS, combining fixation-compatible extracellular labeling with STED and expansion microscopy. The method densely maps architecture from millimeter regional to nanoscopic synaptic scales in rodent and human chemically fixed brains. They reconstruct single synapses and map connectivity by identifying and analyzing putative synaptic clefts. In hippocampal mossy-fiber circuitry, they quantify synaptic input and output structure of identified neurons.
