summaries.advanced: Connectivity is from putative synaptic cleft regions in light microscopy, not from EM-verified synapses. Catalog stages include preparation and synapses; methods are expansion microscopy and super-resolution LM. Human tissue is included as a demonstrated preparation class in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Super-resolution light microscopes can see labeled molecules but often miss the dense packing of all the cells around them. This method stains the spaces between cells so that many cell outlines, and likely contact zones, can be mapped from large regions down to synapses in rodent and human brain tissue.

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila is a genetically accessible model, but publications often document driver-line expression only in one organ system.
ocar.challenge: Whole-body clearing of a small cuticularized larva is full of pitfalls, and many fluorescent proteins do not survive harsh protocols.
ocar.action: Kobler, Weiglein, Hartung, Chen, Gerber, and Thomas optimize a fast, low-cost, low-toxicity clearing protocol for whole-larva multifluorescence, testing fluorescent proteins including monomeric infrared fluorescent protein (mIFP).
ocar.resolution: mIFP is particularly suitable. The protocol supports cellular-resolution light-sheet and confocal imaging, a success rate high enough for small-scale screening, and triple-color imaging with near-infrared, red, and yellow proteins. Example drivers include nsyb-Gal4, IR76b-Gal4, APL-Gal4 and mushroom-body Kenyon cells, and OK371-Gal4.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the method as a way to extend driver documentation systematically to the whole body; that cataloging is enabled, not completed, here.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly maggots are small but have a tough skin, so seeing glowing proteins throughout the whole animal is tricky. This paper gives a quicker, gentler recipe for making the maggot see-through so researchers can check where a genetic switch is on in the entire body.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint (also listed with a Journal of Neurogenetics-style identifier), Kobler, Weiglein, Hartung, Chen, Gerber, and Thomas report a whole-body multifluorescence clearing protocol optimized for Drosophila larvae. They systematically address pitfalls of clearing this cuticularized organism. Among tested fluorescent proteins, monomeric infrared fluorescent protein (mIFP) is particularly suitable. The protocol has low handling time and reduced reagent toxicity, supports light-sheet and confocal imaging at cellular resolution, and allows triple-color imaging (near-infrared, red, yellow). Example expression patterns include nsyb-Gal4, IR76b-Gal4, APL/Kenyon cells, and OK371-Gal4.
summaries.advanced: “Success rate high enough for small-scale screening” is qualitative. Catalog methods include light-sheet and confocal; dataset DS03 Drosophila larva. The work is a visualization protocol, not a connectome. mIFP suitability is relative to the proteins they tested, not a universal ranking of all FPs.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly maggots are small but have a tough skin, so seeing glowing proteins throughout the whole animal is tricky. This paper gives a quicker, gentler recipe for making the maggot see-through so researchers can check where a genetic switch is on in the entire body.

ocar.opportunity: Graph analysis of transcriptomes can reveal communities and modules that might correspond to brain mesostructures and, ultimately, a connectome-like map.
ocar.challenge: It is not obvious which community-detection method yields functional mesostructures, or whether gene-regulatory modules reconstruct known large-scale networks.
ocar.action: Paredes, López, Covantes-Osuna, Ocegueda-Hernández, Romo-Vázquez, and Morales estimate gene communities across Allen Brain Atlas regions, select the method yielding the most functional mesostructures, and build brain-wise region modules as a connectome.
ocar.resolution: Communities map onto cell functions such as neuroplasticity, axonogenesis, and dendritogenesis. Regional modules match previously described circuits including the default mode network and default visual network, supporting the idea that low- and higher-order dynamics originate from modular GRN composition.
ocar.future_work: The match to known networks is correlative from expression communities; causal tests that those GRN modules generate the dynamics are not in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Gene activity differs by brain region, and those patterns can be grouped into communities. This human-atlas study finds gene groups related to growing and reshaping nerve cells, and the way regions cluster together resembles well-known large-scale brain networks.
summaries.intermediate: In Entropy (2021), Paredes, López, Covantes-Osuna, Ocegueda-Hernández, Romo-Vázquez, and Morales propose a bottom-up workflow from gene-regulatory networks to a brain-wise connectome using Allen Brain Atlas transcriptome data. They estimate gene communities across brain regions, choosing the community method that yields the most functional mesostructures, including neuroplasticity, axonogenesis, and dendritogenesis. From those communities they build regional modules representing a connectome, matching previously described anatomical and functional circuits such as the default mode network and default visual network.
summaries.advanced: “Highest number of functional mesostructures” is a selection criterion, not an independent biological gold standard. Correspondence to DMN and a “default visual network” is a match to previously described circuits, not a new imaging validation. Catalog stages: infrastructure, graph analysis; human mesoconnectome from expression, not synapses.

plain_language_summary: Gene activity differs by brain region, and those patterns can be grouped into communities. This human-atlas study finds gene groups related to growing and reshaping nerve cells, and the way regions cluster together resembles well-known large-scale brain networks.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can now produce large 3D volumes in which every subcellular structure and cellular connection can be mapped—connectomics—and that view is useful for degeneration as well as healthy wiring.
ocar.challenge: Conventional EM fields are tiny and sections are far thinner than 100 nm, so seeing a continuum from organelles to tissue context required stitching thousands of large serial sections at full resolution.
ocar.action: Zucker and Dowling review automated large-scale serial-section EM (resolutions of 4 nm or better in cited work) and its application to retina, nerve regeneration, cerebellar rewiring, visual thalamus, and human fovea.
ocar.resolution: At this resolution, chemical synapses, gap junctions, peptides and amines, microcircuits, glia, vasculature, and organelles are all visible. The review argues this continuum of scale is now usable to analyze retinal neural degeneration with connectomics.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a perspective citing others’ volumes (including Kasthuri et al., 2015); it does not itself release a new retinal pathoconnectome.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can now stack thousands of pictures so that an entire neighborhood of the retina can be seen from tiny parts inside cells up to whole circuits. This article explains why that kind of map is useful for studying how retinal cells degenerate.
summaries.intermediate: In Neural Regeneration Research (2021), Zucker and Dowling review large-scale serial-section electron microscopy for connectomics, with emphasis on retinal degeneration. They note that automated technologies now generate reconstructions at 4 nm or better (citing Kasthuri et al., 2015; Baena et al., 2019), resolving excitatory and inhibitory synapses, gap junctions, neuromodulators, microcircuits, glia, vasculature, and organelles. Applications cited include nerve regeneration, cerebellar developmental rewiring, visual thalamus connectivity, and human fovea. The authors position these methods as a way to analyze retinal neural degeneration in 3D.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/perspective. The 4 nm figure is attributed to cited reconstructions, not a new measurement. Catalog datasets include mouse retina and Kasthuri neocortex; the essay is about retinal degeneration using those classes of methods. Organelles and non-neuronal cells are explicitly in scope, not only synapses.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can now stack thousands of pictures so that an entire neighborhood of the retina can be seen from tiny parts inside cells up to whole circuits. This article explains why that kind of map is useful for studying how retinal cells degenerate.

ocar.opportunity: Dense EM wiring diagrams can generate new insights into information processing and storage, especially when combined with activity and behavior—dynamical connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Sparse sampling of connections can miss higher-order structure essential for computation; few systems allow reconstructions plus population activity plus behavior.
ocar.action: Friedrich and Wanner review dense circuit reconstruction in zebrafish, covering brainstem, spinal cord, and olfactory bulb examples.
ocar.resolution: In brainstem, recurrently connected modules can account for slow, low-dimensional integrator dynamics; in spinal cord, connectivity specifies functional differences among premotor interneurons. In olfactory bulb, tuning-dependent connectivity implements whitening by suppressing overrepresented stimulus features. These cases illustrate how dynamical connectomics can reveal circuit mechanisms of higher-order computations.
ocar.future_work: The review points to zebrafish as a uniquely tractable combination of dense structure, activity, and behavior; expanding that triad to more forebrain circuits is the implied program.

summaries.beginner: Knowing every connection is most useful when you can also watch cells fire and see the animal behave. This review of zebrafish work shows examples where dense wiring maps explain slow motor holding, spinal-cord cell roles, and how smell circuits even out overused signals.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Neuroscience (2021), Friedrich and Wanner review dense EM circuit reconstruction in zebrafish as a dynamical-connectomics program combining wiring diagrams, population activity, and behavior. Brainstem examples identify recurrent modules that can account for slow, low-dimensional integrator dynamics. Spinal-cord connectivity specifies functional differences between premotor interneurons. Olfactory-bulb tuning-dependent connectivity implements a whitening transformation via selective suppression of overrepresented stimulus features. The authors argue such higher-order structure cannot be detected by sparse sampling of connectivity.
summaries.advanced: Integrator, whitening, and premotor-function accounts are review-level summaries of the cited circuit papers, not new reconstructions here. Catalog dataset is DS15 zebrafish; method electron microscopy. “Can account for” is a model-level claim for brainstem modules.

plain_language_summary: Knowing every connection is most useful when you can also watch cells fire and see the animal behave. This review of zebrafish work shows examples where dense wiring maps explain slow motor holding, spinal-cord cell roles, and how smell circuits even out overused signals.

ocar.opportunity: Wide-field optical volumes of brain can, in principle, yield 3D neurite reconstructions relevant to disease, including cholinergic neurons in Alzheimer disease.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation, registration of serial sections, and visualization of micrometer-scale neurites in these volumes remain hard; existing tools underperform for this setting.
ocar.action: Ghahremani, Boorboor, Kaufman, and colleagues present NeuroConstruct: an annotation toolbox, CNN neurite segmentation trained on those annotations, thresholding-based soma segmentation, hybrid rendering (iso-surfaces of high-confidence neurites plus a 2D transfer function on classification score versus intensity), and coarse-to-fine serial registration.
ocar.resolution: Quantitative and qualitative analysis is reported to show NeuroConstruct outperforming the state of the art in all design aspects, developed jointly by computer scientists and neuroscientists studying cholinergic neurons.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not name the competing methods or report numeric scores; independent benchmarks on public optical volumes would clarify the SOTA claim.

summaries.beginner: Light-microscope stacks of brain tissue are hard to turn into complete 3D tracings of fine nerve fibers. This software helps experts label examples, trains a computer to find fibers, aligns serial slices, and displays confident tracings together with the raw pictures.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2021), Ghahremani, Boorboor, Mirhosseini, Gudisagar, Ananth, Talmage, Role, and Kaufman introduce NeuroConstruct for wide-field microscopy brain volumes. A Segmentation Toolbox supports expert annotation of micrometer-resolution neurites; CNNs trained on those annotations segment neurites, while somas are segmented by thresholding. Visualization is hybrid: iso-surface rendering of high-confidence neurites plus real-time volume rendering with a 2D transfer function (classification score versus intensity). A Registration Toolbox performs automatic coarse-to-fine alignment of serial sections. The authors report outperformance of prior art on all design aspects, with application to cholinergic neurons affected in Alzheimer disease.
summaries.advanced: “Outperforms the state of the art in all design aspects” is not accompanied by named baselines or metrics in the abstract. Soma segmentation by thresholding may not generalize to crowded or unevenly stained volumes. Application to cholinergic neurons is the motivating collaboration, not a disease-cohort result.

plain_language_summary: Light-microscope stacks of brain tissue are hard to turn into complete 3D tracings of fine nerve fibers. This software helps experts label examples, trains a computer to find fibers, aligns serial slices, and displays confident tracings together with the raw pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Animals survive by translating environmental cues into flexible behavior, and neuropeptides are key integrators of sensory information into output.
ocar.challenge: Peptidergic effects on feeding, mating, sleep, addiction, learning, and locomotion are numerous; a compact nervous system is needed to see mechanisms and conserved disease links.
ocar.action: Bhat, Shahi, Surendran, and Babu review how neuropeptides modulate C. elegans behaviors via neuronal and synaptic signaling, including conserved functions and associated pathophysiology.
ocar.resolution: The review covers mechanisms of neuropeptidergic signaling, how those signals are regulated in different behaviors, and insight toward therapeutics for neuropeptide-related disorders.
ocar.future_work: Therapeutic insight is a stated aim of the review, not a drug-development result.

summaries.beginner: Small signaling proteins help brains change behavior when the world changes. This review uses the worm C. elegans to explain how those peptides affect eating, mating, sleep, learning, and movement, and why that might matter for human disorders.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience (2021), Bhat, Shahi, Surendran, and Babu review neuropeptide modulation of C. elegans behavior. They discuss feeding, mating, sleep, addiction, learning, and locomotion, mechanisms of peptidergic signaling and its regulation, and functions conserved across phyla with associated pathophysiology. The worm’s simple nervous system and connectome are the rationale for mechanistic resolution. The review attempts to provide insight for potential therapeutics of neuropeptide-related disorders.
summaries.advanced: This is a critical review, not new peptidomics. Conservation and pathophysiology are discussed at review level. Catalog dataset DS01 C. elegans. Addiction and therapeutic language should be read as worm-behavior and translational framing, not clinical trials.

plain_language_summary: Small signaling proteins help brains change behavior when the world changes. This review uses the worm C. elegans to explain how those peptides affect eating, mating, sleep, learning, and movement, and why that might matter for human disorders.

ocar.opportunity: A major question is how to relate a connectome to activity, function, and learning; the larval Drosophila olfactory periphery—ORNs in feedback with inhibitory local neurons—is a tractable test.
ocar.challenge: Without a normative theory, observed ORN→LN weights, LN types, and LN–LN connections lack a unified explanation.
ocar.action: Chapochnikov, Pehlevan, and Chklovskii combine structural and activity data in a similarity-matching framework to propose a biologically plausible mechanistic model of the circuit.
ocar.resolution: The model predicts ORN→LN weights found in the connectome, showing they reflect correlations in ORN activity, and explains ORN→LN versus LN–LN weights and the emergence of LN types. The organization can arise through Hebbian plasticity, adapting unsupervised to environments. Functionally, LNs extract redundant correlations and dampen them in ORNs, partially whitening and normalizing stimulus representations.
ocar.future_work: Partial whitening is the proposed function; how complete it is in vivo across odor environments is a prediction to test further.

summaries.beginner: The first smell relay in a fruit-fly maggot has a known wiring map, but it was unclear why the inhibitory cells connect the way they do. This theory-and-data paper argues those connections cancel repeated patterns in incoming smell signals, making later processing easier, and that the wiring can be learned by a simple activity-dependent rule.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint (PNAS-style identifier in the catalog), Chapochnikov, Pehlevan, and Chklovskii model the Drosophila larva peripheral olfactory circuit of ORNs and inhibitory LNs using a similarity-matching normative framework. The model predicts ORN→LN synaptic weights found in the connectome as reflections of ORN activity correlations, and relates ORN→LN and LN–LN weights to the appearance of LN types. Hebbian plasticity can grow this organization unsupervised. Functionally, LNs extract redundant input correlations and dampen them in ORNs, partially whitening and normalizing representations.
summaries.advanced: Connectome weight prediction is a reported match to structure given activity correlations; residual error is not in the abstract. “Partially whitening” is an important qualifier. Catalog dataset DS03 Drosophila larva. The framework is explicitly offered as a way to combine structure, activity, function, and learning—not a unique proof of LN function.

plain_language_summary: The first smell relay in a fruit-fly maggot has a known wiring map, but it was unclear why the inhibitory cells connect the way they do. This theory-and-data paper argues those connections cancel repeated patterns in incoming smell signals, making later processing easier, and that the wiring can be learned by a simple activity-dependent rule.

ocar.opportunity: How sexually dimorphic behavior is encoded is poorly understood when the same neurons are present in both sexes but wired differently.
ocar.challenge: Separating sensory transduction from network topology as the cause of dimorphic nociceptive behavior requires both measurement and a predictive rewiring model.
ocar.action: Pechuk, Goldman, Salzberg, Oren-Suissa, and colleagues characterize dimorphic nociception in C. elegans, compare circuit topology, fit a network model, predict simple rewirings that should switch sex-typical behavior, and test those rewirings, including effects on male mating when aversive cues are present.
ocar.resolution: Sensory transduction is similar between sexes; downstream topology markedly shapes behavior. Predicted subtle synaptic rewirings flip behavior. Rewired males were compromised in finding mating partners when aversive cues were present, suggesting efficient nociceptive avoidance topologies have a reproductive cost.
ocar.future_work: The reproductive-cost interpretation is supported by the mating assay in the abstract; how general it is across other dimorphic circuits is open.

summaries.beginner: Male and female worms can react differently to a nasty touch even if they use the same named sensory cells. This study shows the difference comes mainly from how those cells are wired, and that swapping a few connections can flip one sex’s behavior toward the other’s—while making it harder for males to find mates when danger cues are around.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint, Pechuk, Goldman, Salzberg, Chaubey, Bola, Hoffman, Endreson, Miller, Reger, Portman, Ferkey, Schneidman, and Oren-Suissa study sexually dimorphic nociceptive behavior in C. elegans. Circuits use the same neurons but different wiring. Sensory transduction is similar; network topology markedly shapes behavior. A fitted network model predicts simple rewirings that switch behavior between sexes, and those rewirings experimentally flip behavior. Rewired males were compromised in finding mating partners when aversive cues were present, suggesting a reproductive cost to topologies that enable efficient avoidance.
summaries.advanced: “Subtle synaptic rewirings” is the authors’ description of the predicted interventions. The reproductive-cost claim is tied to the aversive-cue mating assay, not a full fitness measurement. Catalog dataset DS01; stage graph analysis. Model-predicted versus experimentally achieved rewires should be read as a designed test, not a spontaneous evolutionary path.

plain_language_summary: Male and female worms can react differently to a nasty touch even if they use the same named sensory cells. This study shows the difference comes mainly from how those cells are wired, and that swapping a few connections can flip one sex’s behavior toward the other’s—while making it harder for males to find mates when danger cues are around.

ocar.opportunity: Balanced colorings and fibration symmetries reveal clusters of robust synchronization and are abundant in biological networks, including neural ones.
ocar.challenge: Experimental networks are incomplete, so some symmetries are missed; a method is needed to find pseudosymmetries and repair missing or extra edges.
ocar.action: Leifer, Phillips, Sorrentino, and Makse formulate the pseudobalanced coloring integer program (PBCIP) that computes a coloring accounting for missing data and optimally repairs the graph with a minimal number of edge additions/removals, with a Bender’s-decomposition extension for larger networks.
ocar.resolution: Applied to the C. elegans connectome, the repaired graph compares well with a manually curated ground-truth worm graph and with other missing-link-prediction methods.
ocar.future_work: The repair optimizes symmetry under the PBCIP objective; it is not a claim that every added edge is a biological synapse. Larger networks use the decomposition extension.

summaries.beginner: Real wiring maps are missing some links because experiments are incomplete, which can hide repeating patterns. This paper offers a math tool that guesses a few added or removed links to restore those patterns in the worm map, and checks the guesses against a carefully curated version.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Statistical Mechanics (2021), Leifer, Phillips, Sorrentino, and Makse introduce the pseudobalanced coloring problem (PBCIP). An integer program finds a coloring that allows for missing data and repairs the graph with the minimal number of added or removed edges to maximize symmetry. Applied to the C. elegans connectome, the solution compares well with a manually curated ground-truth graph and with other missing-link-prediction methods. Bender’s decomposition extends the algorithm to larger networks.
summaries.advanced: “Compares well” is qualitative in the abstract; numeric precision/recall versus other link predictors is not given. The objective is symmetry maximization under PBCIP, which may not match biological wiring cost. Catalog dataset DS01. Missing-data model is a modeling assumption about incompleteness.

plain_language_summary: Real wiring maps are missing some links because experiments are incomplete, which can hide repeating patterns. This paper offers a math tool that guesses a few added or removed links to restore those patterns in the worm map, and checks the guesses against a carefully curated version.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding a circuit often requires combining morphology, synapse-level connectivity, and—eventually—physiology, which usually live in separate tools.
ocar.challenge: Interactive exploration of connectivity paths on detailed morphologies for simple to medium-complexity circuits is not standard in anatomy-only viewers.
ocar.action: Galindo, Toharia, Robles, and Pastor present SynCoPa, with visual metaphors for synapses and interconnection paths overlaid on detailed neuron morphologies.
ocar.resolution: The tool is designed for interactive exploration of connectivity elements and paths, helping hypotheses about synapse spatial distributions, how neurons connect, and morphology–connectivity relationships. It is described as easily extendable to functional data from simulators such as NEURON and Arbor.
ocar.future_work: Extension to simulation data is presented as straightforward but not demonstrated as a completed coupled pipeline in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Wiring lists and 3D cell shapes are often shown in different programs, which makes paths through a circuit hard to see. This visualization tool draws the contacts and the routes between cells on top of detailed shapes so a person can explore a small or medium circuit interactively.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2021), Galindo, Toharia, Robles, and Pastor present SynCoPa for visualizing connectivity paths and synapses over detailed morphologies. Aimed at simple to medium-complexity circuits at connectome level, it uses visual metaphors for synapses and paths combined with morphological rendering. Intended uses include hypotheses about synapse spatial distributions, connection patterns, and morphology–connectivity relationships. The authors say it is easily extendable to functional data from morphologically detailed simulators such as NEURON and Arbor.
summaries.advanced: This is a visualization-methods paper; no user-study metrics appear in the abstract. “Simple to medium complexity” is the stated scope. Simulator integration is prospective. Catalog stages: infrastructure, graph analysis, modeling.

plain_language_summary: Wiring lists and 3D cell shapes are often shown in different programs, which makes paths through a circuit hard to see. This visualization tool draws the contacts and the routes between cells on top of detailed shapes so a person can explore a small or medium circuit interactively.

ocar.opportunity: Diffusion MRI tractography is the only noninvasive human structural-connectome method, but validation has shown mistracking as local orientation errors accumulate along long streamlines.
ocar.challenge: Separating that length bias from genuine spatial embedding of brain topology requires a modality that is not tractography, plus geometric nulls.
ocar.action: Trinkle, Foxley, Wildenberg, Kasthuri, and La Rivière compare ex vivo mouse tractography graphs and Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas tracer graphs to random geometric surrogate graphs that preserve low-order distance effects, and they compare two streamline-to-node assignment strategies.
ocar.resolution: Geometry plays a substantially larger role in tractography graphs than in tracer graphs. Tractography underestimates long-distance weights, placing hubs near the geometric center as geometric surrogates do, whereas tracer graphs place hubs more peripherally in cortex. Assignment-strategy differences are small relative to tractography-versus-tracer differences.
ocar.future_work: The authors promote geometric benchmarking in future tractography validation; human in vivo generalization is not claimed from this ex vivo mouse study.

summaries.beginner: MRI can estimate brain cables in living people, but those estimates often go wrong over long distances. By comparing MRI-style tracing with real tracer injections in mouse, this study shows that MRI maps are shaped more by simple distance rules—and put their hubs too close to the middle of the brain.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2021), Trinkle, Foxley, Wildenberg, Kasthuri, and La Rivière compare mouse ex vivo tractography graphs with neural-tracer graphs from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, each against random geometric surrogates that preserve low-order distance effects. Geometry contributes more to tractography topology than to tracer topology. Tractography underestimates long-distance weights and places hubs near the geometric center, matching its geometric surrogates, while tracer graphs place hubs further into peripheral cortex. Two streamline node-assignment strategies differ little compared with the tractography–tracer gap. Analyses also cover modularity and efficiency.
summaries.advanced: Findings are mouse ex vivo tractography versus Allen tracers, not human in vivo MRI. “Substantially larger role” of geometry is the authors’ comparison of graph properties to geometric nulls. Hub location is a reported topological consequence of length bias. Catalog stages: preparation, graph analysis; organism mouse.

plain_language_summary: MRI can estimate brain cables in living people, but those estimates often go wrong over long distances. By comparing MRI-style tracing with real tracer injections in mouse, this study shows that MRI maps are shaped more by simple distance rules—and put their hubs too close to the middle of the brain.

ocar.opportunity: Activity-dependent sculpting of circuits is classic in mammals; Drosophila was long thought to specify its connectome largely via genetically hardwired recognition molecules.
ocar.challenge: That contrast left open whether activity is a fundamental, shared aspect of brain development or a mammalian specialty.
ocar.action: Akin and Zipursky review recent findings that activity during development also contributes to circuit assembly in the fly.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that activity is a fundamental aspect of brain development in general, and that Drosophila’s toolkit for circuit development, structure, and function offers opportunities to study the phenomenon.
ocar.future_work: The review invites mechanistic work in the fly; it does not itself quantify how much of the connectome is activity-dependent versus molecularly specified.

summaries.beginner: It used to be thought that fly brains are wired mostly by genetic name tags, while mammal brains also use nerve-cell activity to sculpt circuits. This short review summarizes new evidence that activity helps build fly circuits too, so the two stories are more alike than they seemed.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Genetics and Development (2020), Akin and Zipursky review evidence that neural activity during development contributes to Drosophila circuit assembly. They contrast this with the earlier view that genetically hardwired cell-recognition molecules suffice to specify the fly connectome, unlike activity-dependent mammalian development. They argue activity is a fundamental aspect of brain development generally, and highlight opportunities in the fly toolkit for examining circuit development, structure, and function.
summaries.advanced: This is a short opinion/review, not a new activity-block experiment. The “generally thought” historical framing is the authors’. Partitioning the connectome into activity-dependent versus recognition-molecule-dependent fractions is not numerically attempted.

plain_language_summary: It used to be thought that fly brains are wired mostly by genetic name tags, while mammal brains also use nerve-cell activity to sculpt circuits. This short review summarizes new evidence that activity helps build fly circuits too, so the two stories are more alike than they seemed.

ocar.opportunity: First-order thalamocortical synapses in primary sensory cortex are comparatively well studied; higher-order thalamic projections to higher-order cortex are not.
ocar.challenge: Labeling that projection without retrograde contamination, then measuring ultrastructure across layers, needs a specific EM-visible strategy.
ocar.action: Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri use an intersectional viral cocktail (cre plus cre-dependent ascorbate peroxidase) in mouse posterior medial nucleus to label thalamocortical axons and synapses in secondary somatosensory cortex, analyzed with large-volume serial EM.
ocar.resolution: Labeled synapses were 14% of all synapses in the volume, consistent with prior first-order estimates. Labeled terminals were larger, more often mitochondrial, more likely to hit spiny rather than aspiny dendrites, and often innervated larger spines with spine apparatuses. Labeled terminals were more prevalent in layers 2/3, where labeled-versus-unlabeled differences were greatest—contrasting reports from first-order pathways where layer-4 terminals were larger than those in 2/3.
ocar.future_work: The authors say this is a first glimpse of higher-order thalamocortical ultrastructure and that more analyses are needed, because such connectivity likely represents a majority of thalamocortical circuitry.

summaries.beginner: Much of what we know about thalamic contacts on cortex comes from the first, primary sensory stop, not from later “higher-order” thalamic stations. This mouse electron-microscope study labels those later fibers into a secondary touch area and finds they prefer upper layers and look different from unlabeled contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In the European Journal of Neuroscience (2020), Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri label the projection from mouse posterior medial nucleus to secondary somatosensory cortex with an intersectional viral APEX approach, avoiding retrograde labeling, and reconstruct synapses with large-volume serial EM. Labeled thalamocortical synapses were 14% of all synapses in the volume. Labeled terminals were larger, more often contained mitochondria, preferentially targeted spiny dendrites, and often innervated larger spines with spine apparatuses. They were more prevalent in layers 2/3, where differences from unlabeled terminals were greatest, unlike first-order motifs emphasizing layer 4 (Viaene et al., 2011a).
summaries.advanced: 14% is the fraction in this cortical volume, described as consistent with previous first-order estimates—not a brain-wide average. “First glimpse” is the authors’ claim for higher-order TC ultrastructure. Catalog dataset DS12 L4 barrel cortex may not match S2 higher-order sampling; ground claims in POm→S2 as stated. Intersectional labeling is argued to be free of retrograde contamination.

plain_language_summary: Much of what we know about thalamic contacts on cortex comes from the first, primary sensory stop, not from later “higher-order” thalamic stations. This mouse electron-microscope study labels those later fibers into a secondary touch area and finds they prefer upper layers and look different from unlabeled contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-cell organelle organization is central to cell biology but requires nanometer 3D reconstruction of entire cells and then characterization of many structure classes.
ocar.challenge: Dataset size and the number of structures make fully manual analysis impractical; methods must generalize across cell types.
ocar.action: Heinrich, Bennett, Ackerman, Saalfeld, Weigel, and colleagues train deep-learning architectures on diverse FIB-SEM samples (4 or 8 nm/voxel, near-isotropic) to automatically reconstruct 35 organelle classes, from ER to microtubules to ribosomes, and launch the OpenOrganelle repository.
ocar.resolution: Automatic reconstructions support previously inaccessible metrics, including spatial interactions, and can automatically register light and electron microscopy for correlative studies. Data, code, and trained models are shared so others can query and further reconstruct the datasets.
ocar.future_work: OpenOrganelle is an invitation to further reconstruction; 35 classes is the trained set, not every cellular structure.

summaries.beginner: A cell is packed with dozens of kinds of tiny machines, and drawing them all by hand in a 3D electron-microscope volume is unrealistic. This project trains computers to outline 35 kinds of cell parts in whole cells and posts the pictures, code, and models for anyone to use.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Heinrich, Bennett, Ackerman, Park, Bogovic, Eckstein, Petruncio, Clements, Xu, Funke, Korff, Hess, Lippincott-Schwartz, Saalfeld, and Weigel present a pipeline for automatic whole-cell organelle segmentation in FIB-SEM at 4 or 8 nm per voxel. Deep-learning architectures trained on diverse samples reconstruct 35 organelle classes, enabling quantification of spatial interactions and automatic LM–EM registration. They release OpenOrganelle as an open data and code repository for the datasets, models, and further reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: 35 classes and 4 or 8 nm voxels are the stated scope. “Previously inaccessible metrics” are enabled by automation; specific numeric biology findings are not listed in the abstract. Training on diverse samples is the generalization strategy. Catalog method FIB-SEM; stages include sectioning, acquisition, segmentation.

plain_language_summary: A cell is packed with dozens of kinds of tiny machines, and drawing them all by hand in a 3D electron-microscope volume is unrealistic. This project trains computers to outline 35 kinds of cell parts in whole cells and posts the pictures, code, and models for anyone to use.

ocar.opportunity: Supervised EM segmentation models fail to generalize across unrelated datasets, while unsupervised methods need relevant pre-training images.
ocar.challenge: Existing EM collections are large and homogeneous, so pre-training is computationally expensive and shows little value for unseen biological contexts.
ocar.action: Conrad and Narayan curate CEM500K: a 25 GB set of 0.5 × 10^6 unique cellular EM images from nearly 600 3D and 10,000 2D images across more than 100 unrelated projects, then pre-train models and evaluate transfer on six public plus one new segmentation benchmarks.
ocar.resolution: CEM500K-pretrained models learn biologically relevant, augmentation-resilient features and achieve state-of-the-art on each of the seven transfer tasks. Dataset, models, and curation pipeline are released.
ocar.future_work: The authors invite community expansion of the curation pipeline; SOTA is reported on the seven evaluated tasks, not every future EM problem.

summaries.beginner: Computers trained to outline cell parts in one electron-microscope project often fail on the next, because the training pictures were all too similar. This paper gathers a half-million varied cell images so that a computer can learn more general visual features and then do better on new outlining jobs.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint (eLife DOI in the catalog), Conrad and Narayan introduce CEM500K, a 25 GB dataset of 0.5 million unique cellular EM images curated from nearly 600 3D and 10,000 2D images from more than 100 unrelated projects. Models pre-trained on CEM500K learn features that are biologically relevant and resilient to meaningful augmentations. Transfer learning reports state-of-the-art results on six public benchmarks and one newly derived segmentation task. Data and code are released via EMPIAR and GitHub.
summaries.advanced: 0.5 × 10^6 unique images and 25 GB are the scale figures; “nimble” contrasts with larger homogeneous EM corpora. SOTA is claimed on the seven listed transfer tasks. Unsupervised/pre-training value is specifically for unseen biological contexts versus homogeneous pre-training. Catalog stages: segmentation, proofreading; method electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: Computers trained to outline cell parts in one electron-microscope project often fail on the next, because the training pictures were all too similar. This paper gathers a half-million varied cell images so that a computer can learn more general visual features and then do better on new outlining jobs.

ocar.opportunity: Neuronal morphologies underlie electrical behavior, connectomes, and brain dynamics, but biological reconstructions are too few for comprehensive cell-type models and disease-altered structure.
ocar.challenge: Digitally synthesizing dendrites that remain statistically faithful in morpho-electrical properties and connectivity is unsolved if generators ignore topology.
ocar.action: Kanari, Dictus, Chalimourda, Markram, and colleagues apply a topological descriptor that categorizes dendritic morphologies to synthesize cortical dendrites, then build a synthesized cortical column from reference cells of all layers and morphological types.
ocar.resolution: Synthesized dendrites are statistically indistinguishable from reconstructions in morpho-electrical properties and connectivity. The synthesized column’s connectome is almost indistinguishable from the reconstructed column’s. Topology-guided synthesis enables rapid digital reconstruction of regions from relatively few reference cells and can incorporate disease-associated dendritic alterations to study network-level consequences.
ocar.future_work: The method still depends on having reference reconstructions per type; it does not replace experimental sampling of rare or pathological types not in the reference set.

summaries.beginner: There are not enough fully traced neurons to build a whole cortical column from real cells alone. This method copies the branching style of real dendrites to grow extra digital cells that still connect like the originals, so large networks can be studied in the computer.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Kanari, Dictus, Chalimourda, Van Geit, Coste, Shillcock, Hess, and Markram use a topological barcode of dendritic shape to synthesize cortical dendrites. Synthesized cells are reported as statistically indistinguishable from reconstructions in morpho-electrical properties and connectivity. From reference cells of all layers and morphological types they build a synthesized cortical column whose connectome is almost indistinguishable from that of reconstructed cells. The approach is aimed at rapid digital reconstruction from few reference cells and at probing how dendritic alterations associated with medical conditions change large-scale networks.
summaries.advanced: “Statistically indistinguishable” and “almost indistinguishable” connectomes are the authors’ claims; test names and p-values are not in the abstract. Synthesis is topology-guided from reconstructed examples, so bias in the reference set propagates. Disease-related networks are an application mode, not a patient dataset here. Catalog stage graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: There are not enough fully traced neurons to build a whole cortical column from real cells alone. This method copies the branching style of real dendrites to grow extra digital cells that still connect like the originals, so large networks can be studied in the computer.

ocar.opportunity: The mammalian rod bipolar pathway is among the best-studied retinal circuits, but its synaptic interactions with other circuits remain unresolved.
ocar.challenge: Which interneuron type supplies most inhibition to Aii amacrine cells, the hub of night vision, was not established.
ocar.action: Park, Lieberman, Ke, Demb, Singer, and colleagues combine mouse-retina anatomy and physiology, then use nNOS-CreER to confirm the interneuron as the wide-field NOS-1 amacrine cell.
ocar.resolution: A single multistratified, axon-bearing GABAergic AC type, with dendrites in ON and OFF layers but a pure ON (depolarizing) light response, provides the majority of synaptic inhibition to Aii cells. The authors identify NOS-1 as this cell and conclude it mediates long-range inhibition during night vision and is a major element of the rod bipolar pathway.
ocar.future_work: The study demonstrates that targeted connectomics can identify novel circuits; how NOS-1 inhibition interacts with degeneration-related Aii rewiring is outside this abstract.

summaries.beginner: Night vision in mammals depends on a well-known chain of retinal cells, but it was unclear which cell supplies most of the “brakes” on a key link in that chain. This mouse study finds that one wide-field inhibitory cell type does most of that job and helps carry inhibition over long distances in the dark.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Park, Lieberman, Ke, Rho, Ghorbani, Rahmani, Jun, Lee, Kim, Briggman, Demb, and Singer combine anatomical and physiological analyses in mouse retina. They find that the majority of synaptic inhibition to Aii amacrine cells comes from a single multistratified, axon-bearing GABAergic amacrine type with dendrites in ON and OFF layers but a pure ON depolarizing light response. Using nNOS-CreER, they confirm this interneuron as the wide-field NOS-1 amacrine cell, concluding it mediates long-range inhibition during night vision and is a major rod-bipolar-pathway element.
summaries.advanced: “Majority of synaptic inhibition” is the connectomic/physiological claim to Aii; other inhibitory sources are not quantified in the abstract. ON dendrites in OFF layers versus pure ON physiology is an explicit mixed anatomy/physiology feature. Catalog dataset DS09/DS10 mouse retina. Targeted connectomics is offered as a general identification strategy.

plain_language_summary: Night vision in mammals depends on a well-known chain of retinal cells, but it was unclear which cell supplies most of the “brakes” on a key link in that chain. This mouse study finds that one wide-field inhibitory cell type does most of that job and helps carry inhibition over long distances in the dark.

ocar.opportunity: A wiring diagram is a prerequisite for understanding function, analogous to a genome, but it remains under-used without physiological validation of synapses.
ocar.challenge: Larval Drosophila electrophysiology is uncommon and equipment-heavy, so connectivity is often inferred from behavior or GCaMP, which have important limitations for proving monosynaptic connections.
ocar.action: Giachello, Zarin, Kohsaka, Fan, Nose, Landgraf, and Baines use electrophysiology to test driver lines reported to label premotor interneurons that the Drosophila connectome project suggests are monosynaptically connected to the aCC motoneuron.
ocar.resolution: Results validate monosynaptic connectivity for four selected lines, and highlight the need to functionally validate driver lines before use.
ocar.future_work: Only four lines are validated here; the broader connectome’s suggested premotor set still needs similar tests.

summaries.beginner: A wiring map can suggest that cell A touches cell B, but a direct electrical test is the gold standard. This fruit-fly larva study checks four genetic lines that were supposed to label cells one step upstream of a known motor neuron and confirms those direct connections.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Giachello, Zarin, Kohsaka, Fan, Nose, Landgraf, and Baines electrophysiologically validate premotor interneurons proposed by the Drosophila larval connectome to be monosynaptically connected to the anterior corner cell (aCC) motoneuron. They argue that behavior and GCaMP imaging have limitations for this purpose. Four selected driver lines are validated as labeling such premotor interneurons. The study also stresses validating driver lines before use.
summaries.advanced: Validation is for four selected lines, not the full premotor census. Electrophysiology is presented as necessary because GCaMP and behavior lack the temporal/spatial resolution to map synaptic connectivity. Catalog dataset DS03 Drosophila larva. Negative results on other lines are not described in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: A wiring map can suggest that cell A touches cell B, but a direct electrical test is the gold standard. This fruit-fly larva study checks four genetic lines that were supposed to label cells one step upstream of a known motor neuron and confirms those direct connections.

ocar.opportunity: Nematode function is usually read from the synaptic connectome, but extrasynaptic volume transmission (EVT) could allow communication without synapses, as in other invertebrates.
ocar.challenge: EVT had been discussed for C. elegans, yet no experiment had identified pseudocoelomic fluid as a vehicle for neuropeptides or biogenic amines. In Ascaris suum, FLP-18 peptides strongly stimulate female reproductive muscle despite being expressed only in anatomically distant cells with no known synapses onto that tissue.
ocar.action: Atkinson, Liu, Beets, Li, Mousley, and colleagues analyze A. suum pseudocoelomic fluid (As-PCF) peptidomics and test As-PCF on muscle, C. elegans FLP-18 receptors, and C. elegans behavior.
ocar.resolution: As-PCF contains FLPs and neuropeptide-like proteins; As-FLP-18A dominates the peptidome. As-PCF potently modulates nematode reproductive muscle ex vivo, mirroring synthetic FLP-18, activates C. elegans NPR-4 and NPR-5, and alters C. elegans behavior. FLP-18 and its receptors show pan-phylum distribution in nematodes.
ocar.future_work: This is presented as the first direct experimental evidence for an extrasynaptic volume route in nematodes; mapping how general EVT is across behaviors and species remains open.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring maps show cell-to-cell contacts, but chemicals might also travel in the body fluid to reach distant organs. This study finds peptide messengers in that fluid in a parasitic worm, and the fluid can make reproductive muscle contract and can change behavior in C. elegans, even without a direct nerve contact.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Atkinson, Liu, McKay, Vandewyer, Viau, Irvine, Rosa, Li, Marks, Maule, Mitreva, Beets, Li, and Mousley report extrasynaptic volume transmission of neuropeptides in nematodes. Ascaris suum pseudocoelomic fluid (As-PCF) contains FMRFamide-like peptides and neuropeptide-like proteins, with As-FLP-18A dominating. As-PCF potently modulates reproductive muscle ex vivo like synthetic FLP-18, activates C. elegans FLP-18 receptors NPR-4 and NPR-5, and alters C. elegans behavior. FLP-18 and receptors are pan-phylum in nematodes. The authors argue this is the first direct evidence that PCF is an EVT route, relevant to receptor deorphanization and anthelmintic discovery.
summaries.advanced: “First direct experimental evidence” is the authors’ claim. Dominance of As-FLP-18A is a peptidomic result; other peptides are present. Receptor activation is in C. elegans NPRs, while the fluid is from Ascaris—cross-species pharmacology. Catalog dataset DS01 C. elegans; the primary fluid is A. suum. Drug-discovery framing is translational, not a compound screen result in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring maps show cell-to-cell contacts, but chemicals might also travel in the body fluid to reach distant organs. This study finds peptide messengers in that fluid in a parasitic worm, and the fluid can make reproductive muscle contract and can change behavior in C. elegans, even without a direct nerve contact.

ocar.opportunity: Comparing whole-brain functional data across animals requires naming cells in dense image stacks, but unbiased identification is difficult and expert-dependent.
ocar.challenge: Existing methods struggle under the noise and packing typical of experimental C. elegans whole-brain images, and building atlases or adding features is often computationally heavy.
ocar.action: Chaudhary, Lee, Li, Patel, and Lu present CRF_ID, a conditional random field framework that maximizes intrinsic shape similarity, with efficient atlas building from annotated data and easy addition of new features (e.g., new strains).
ocar.resolution: CRF_ID achieves higher accuracy than existing methods on simulated and ground-truth experimental datasets and is more robust to challenging noise. They demonstrate annotation across strains, orientations, and tasks including gene-expression localization and multi-cellular and whole-brain functional imaging.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest the approach may be valuable for other systems’ dense annotation tasks; those transfers are not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: In a packed picture of a worm brain, even experts disagree on which glowing blob is which named cell. This software uses cell shapes and a statistical model to name cells more accurately and with less human bias, and it works across worm strains and imaging tasks.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint (eLife DOI in the catalog), Chaudhary, Lee, Li, Patel, and Lu introduce CRF_ID, a conditional-random-field framework for automated cell-identity annotation in dense images. It maximizes intrinsic shape similarity, outperforms existing methods on simulated and ground-truth experimental data, and is more robust to experimental noise. Atlases can be built efficiently from annotated data, and new features (for example from new strains) can be added easily. Demonstrations in C. elegans include gene-expression localization and multi-cellular and whole-brain functional imaging, across strains and animal orientations.
summaries.advanced: “Higher accuracy” and “better robustness” are claimed versus existing methods; numeric accuracies are not in the abstract. Scope of demonstrations is C. elegans; other systems are a suggested extension. Catalog stages include proofreading, infrastructure, graph analysis, modeling; dataset DS01.

plain_language_summary: In a packed picture of a worm brain, even experts disagree on which glowing blob is which named cell. This software uses cell shapes and a statistical model to name cells more accurately and with less human bias, and it works across worm strains and imaging tasks.

ocar.opportunity: Gap junctions in the Aii–ON cone bipolar network are essential for night vision, modulate day vision, and contribute to impairment in retinal degenerations, so their extended topology matters.
ocar.challenge: Neither the extended coupling network among ON CBCs nor its conservation was well established, and connectomics often under-detects gap junctions.
ocar.action: Sigulinsky, Anderson, Marc, Jones, and colleagues map gap junctions in a high-resolution connectomics dataset of adult female rabbit retina.
ocar.resolution: Gap junctions are 5%–25% of ON CBC axonal synaptic contacts. Canonical Aii-to-ON CBC rod-signal transfer is conserved, including uneven Aii distribution and one ON CBC class lacking direct Aii coupling. Unexpectedly, most ON CBC gap junctions are with other ON CBCs, creating many lateral paths within and across parallel streams, with precise partnership rules rivaling chemical-synapse specificity, including size and spatial topologies.
ocar.future_work: These motifs extend the coupled Aii–ON CBC network for both scotopic and photopic processing and for disease; therapeutic implications are noted but not tested here.

summaries.beginner: Besides chemical contacts, retinal cells are also linked by tiny electrical pores. Mapping those pores in a rabbit retina shows that night-vision cells follow expected rules, but most of the electrical links actually join similar bipolar cells to each other, creating many side roads between parallel visual channels.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Neuroscience (2020), Sigulinsky, Anderson, Kerzner, Rapp, Pfeiffer, Rodman, Emrich, Rapp, Nelson, Lauritzen, Meyer, Marc, and Jones map gap junctions in an adult female rabbit-retina connectome. Gap junctions constitute 5%–25% of all axonal synaptic contacts of ON cone bipolar classes. Canonical Aii-to-ON CBC rod-signal coupling is conserved, including uneven Aii distribution and one class without direct Aii coupling. Most ON CBC gap junctions are with other ON CBCs, forming an interconnected network with lateral paths within and across parallel streams. Coupling follows precise partnership, size, and spatial rulesets comparable in specificity to chemical synapses.
summaries.advanced: 5%–25% is the range across ON CBC classes, not a single fraction. “Unexpectedly” majority CBC–CBC coupling is the headline revision of Aii-centric intuition. Dataset is rabbit; catalog tags DS09/DS10 mouse retina—ground the science in rabbit. Detection of gap junctions is a stated reason connectomics studies must include them. Female adult retina is the sample.

plain_language_summary: Besides chemical contacts, retinal cells are also linked by tiny electrical pores. Mapping those pores in a rabbit retina shows that night-vision cells follow expected rules, but most of the electrical links actually join similar bipolar cells to each other, creating many side roads between parallel visual channels.

ocar.opportunity: Rodents use whiskers to detect stimuli, distinguish texture, locate objects, and navigate, and much of that computation is thought to occur in barrel cortex (wS1), where each whisker maps to an anatomical barrel.
ocar.challenge: A causal, mechanistic account requires jointly understanding pathways to wS1, excitatory and inhibitory cell classes, local and long-range synapses, neuromodulation, and cell-type-specific activity during behavior.
ocar.action: Staiger and Petersen review signaling pathways from whiskers to wS1 and current knowledge of excitatory and inhibitory types, microcircuit and long-range connectivity, neuromodulators, and links from connectivity to activity in whisker behaviors.
ocar.resolution: Cell classes can be defined by anatomy, electrophysiology, and molecules; synaptic connectivity and neuromodulation are beginning to be understood; recent methods relate cell-type-specific connectivity to activity during behavior.
ocar.future_work: They identify as a goal a causal mechanistic understanding of how selected tactile features are processed by specific neuron types in synaptically defined networks and signaled downstream for sensory-guided decisions.

summaries.beginner: Mice and rats explore with their whiskers, and each whisker has its own patch of cortex. This long review gathers what is known about the cell types in those patches, how they connect, and how they fire when the animal uses its whiskers, and it lists what is still needed to explain decisions based on touch.
summaries.intermediate: In Physiological Reviews (2020), Staiger and Petersen review neuronal circuits in rodent barrel cortex for whisker sensory perception. They cover pathways from whiskers to wS1, classification of excitatory and inhibitory neurons by anatomy, electrophysiology, and molecules, local microcircuit and long-range connectivity, neuromodulation, and cell-type-specific activity during whisker-related behaviors. The barrel map is highlighted as allowing precise study of sensory processing in a well-defined topography. They outline the goal of causal mechanistic understanding of tactile feature processing and downstream decision-making.
summaries.advanced: This is a comprehensive review, not a new connectome. “Beginning to be understood” qualifies connectivity and neuromodulation. Catalog dataset DS12 L4 barrel cortex; organism mouse (review is rodent wS1 generally). Causal understanding is explicitly a future goal.

plain_language_summary: Mice and rats explore with their whiskers, and each whisker has its own patch of cortex. This long review gathers what is known about the cell types in those patches, how they connect, and how they fire when the animal uses its whiskers, and it lists what is still needed to explain decisions based on touch.

ocar.opportunity: Computational models of cognition need mesoconnectomes with laminar and cell-class specificity, which are extremely hard to measure directly.
ocar.challenge: Whether gene-expression patterns can predict cell-class- and layer-specific axonal projections—and what those predictive genes do—is an open multimodal-integration problem.
ocar.action: Timonidis, Bakker, and Tiesinga train models on public volumetric gene-expression and connectivity data to predict cell-class- and layer-specific projections from individual genes and from 200 spatial gene modules obtained by dictionary learning and sparse coding, plus binarized projections.
ocar.resolution: Ridge (L2) regression had the highest cross-validated accuracy, median r² = 0.54, corresponding to median ROC AUC 0.89 for binarized predictions. Spatial modules reached median r² = 0.51. Gene-ontology enrichment of the most predictive genes highlighted postsynaptic function.
ocar.future_work: They present a workflow for multimodal integration to improve mesoconnectome accuracy; residual unexplained variance (1 − 0.54) remains large for some targets.

summaries.beginner: We rarely know every connection of every cell class in a mouse brain, but we do have maps of gene activity. This study trains computers to guess layer- and cell-class-specific wiring from those gene maps, and the guesses are better than chance, especially for whether a projection is present or absent.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroinformatics (2020), Timonidis, Bakker, and Tiesinga predict a cell-class-specific mouse mesoconnectome from gene-expression data. Ridge regression achieved the highest cross-validated accuracy (median r² 0.54; median ROC AUC 0.89 for binarized projections). Two hundred spatial gene modules from dictionary learning and sparse coding predicted with median r² 0.51. Gene-ontology enrichment of the most predictive gene groups yielded significant annotations related to postsynaptic function. The workflow is offered for multimodal data integration to improve mesoconnectome accuracy.
summaries.advanced: Median r² 0.54 means much variance is still unexplained; AUC 0.89 is for binarized presence/absence, a different task than strength. Module-based prediction is comparable, not superior. Public volumetric expression and connectivity are the sources; cell-class labels inherit those resources’ limitations. Catalog organism mouse.

plain_language_summary: We rarely know every connection of every cell class in a mouse brain, but we do have maps of gene activity. This study trains computers to guess layer- and cell-class-specific wiring from those gene maps, and the guesses are better than chance, especially for whether a projection is present or absent.

ocar.opportunity: 3D and large-FOV imaging make acquisition time a bottleneck, and dose must be reduced for radiation-sensitive biological tissue.
ocar.challenge: Random sparse scanning plus reconstruction must still support the neuron-segmentation tasks that connectomics cares about, not only pretty images.
ocar.action: Potocek, Trampert, Peemen, Schoenmakers, and Dahmen demonstrate SEM sparse acquisition, reconstruction by compressive sensing or neural networks, then deep-learning segmentation of neurons from the reconstructions.
ocar.resolution: Average dwell time per pixel can be reduced by a factor of 2–3, providing real-life confirmation of prior simulated-data results in a key connectomics segmentation application and showing feasibility of random sparse scanning in this scenario.
ocar.future_work: The factor of 2–3 is for this workflow; limits at still-sparser sampling or other tissues are not specified.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope cameras can skip many pixels to save time and reduce damage, then a computer fills in the gaps. This study shows that those filled-in pictures are still good enough for a second computer to outline neurons, cutting average exposure about two- to threefold.
summaries.intermediate: In Microscopy and Microanalysis (2020), Potocek, Trampert, Peemen, Schoenmakers, and Dahmen combine random sparse SEM scanning with reconstruction (compressive sensing or neural networks) and then automatically segment neurons with deep learning. They report that average dwell time per pixel can be reduced by a factor of 2–3. The work is presented as real-life confirmation of earlier simulated-data results for a key connectomics segmentation application.
summaries.advanced: The 2–3× dwell-time reduction is the headline; segmentation accuracy versus fully sampled data is not numerically reported in the abstract. Reconstruction can be CS or NNs; which is better is not specified here. Catalog stages: acquisition, segmentation, modeling; method SEM.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope cameras can skip many pixels to save time and reduce damage, then a computer fills in the gaps. This study shows that those filled-in pictures are still good enough for a second computer to outline neurons, cutting average exposure about two- to threefold.

ocar.opportunity: New male and hermaphrodite C. elegans chemical connectomes allow a statistical look at unidirectional versus reciprocal synapses.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear how reciprocal connections contribute to communication, synaptic multiplicity, and sex differences among shared neurons.
ocar.action: Wright and Goltsev analyze unidirectional and reciprocally connected pairs in the published male and hermaphrodite chemical connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Reciprocal connections provide communication between most neurons with chemical synapses and comprise on average more synapses than unidirectional connections and than the entire connectome. Afferent connections onto high in-degree neurons have above-average synaptic multiplicity, increasing with in-degree. The male forms two times fewer reciprocal connections between sex-shared neurons than the hermaphrodite, but many reciprocal connections with male-specific neurons; the authors interpret this as evidence for Hebbian structural plasticity.
ocar.future_work: Hebbian plasticity is an interpretation of the multiplicity and reciprocity statistics, not a developmental time series.

summaries.beginner: Some worm cells contact each other in both directions, others only one way. Counting those patterns in male and hermaphrodite wiring maps, this paper finds that two-way contacts are richer and that males and hermaphrodites differ in how they use two-way contacts among shared cells.
summaries.intermediate: In the European Journal of Neuroscience (2020), Wright and Goltsev statistically analyze unidirectional and reciprocal chemical connections in male and hermaphrodite C. elegans connectomes. Reciprocal connections provide communication between most chemically synapsing neurons and have on average more synapses than unidirectional connections and than the connectome overall. Afferent synapses onto high in-degree neurons show above-average multiplicity that increases with in-degree. Males have two times fewer reciprocal connections among sex-shared neurons than hermaphrodites, but many reciprocal connections involving male-specific neurons. These observations are taken as evidence for Hebbian structural plasticity.
summaries.advanced: “Two times fewer” is the male versus hermaphrodite comparison for sex-shared reciprocal connections. Multiplicity–in-degree correlation is a structural finding; Hebbian plasticity is an inference. Analysis is chemical connectomes as in the cited new data, not gap junctions. Catalog dataset DS01.

plain_language_summary: Some worm cells contact each other in both directions, others only one way. Counting those patterns in male and hermaphrodite wiring maps, this paper finds that two-way contacts are richer and that males and hermaphrodites differ in how they use two-way contacts among shared cells.

ocar.opportunity: Biological network studies often test whether motifs are over-represented, linking them to function.
ocar.challenge: There is disagreement about motif significance, and standard tests have shortcomings; exponential random graph models (ERGMs) can address some of them but were historically hard to fit on large networks.
ocar.action: Stivala and Lomi illustrate ERGMs on an undirected protein–protein interaction network and directed gene-regulatory networks, using improved estimation algorithms.
ocar.resolution: ERGMs indicate triangle over-representation in the PPI network and confirm prior research on transitive-triangle (feed-forward loop) over-representation in E. coli and yeast regulatory networks. Under-representation of cyclic triangles (feedback loops) can be explained as a consequence of other topological features.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a methods illustration on PPI and GRN graphs, not an EM connectome motif analysis; applying the same ERGMs to synapse-resolution connectomes is a natural extension not shown here.

summaries.beginner: Biologists often ask whether a small wiring pattern appears more than chance would allow. This paper shows a statistical model that can test those patterns more carefully than older methods, using protein-interaction and gene-control networks as examples.
summaries.intermediate: In Applied Network Science (2020), Stivala and Lomi apply exponential random graph models to test biological motif significance, arguing ERGMs overcome some shortcomings of common tests and that estimation advances now allow larger networks. On an undirected PPI network, ERGMs indicate triangle over-representation. On directed E. coli and yeast gene-regulatory networks, they confirm over-representation of transitive triangles (feed-forward loops). Under-representation of cyclic triangles (feedback loops) can be explained as a consequence of other topological features.
summaries.advanced: Confirmation of prior FFL results is relative to earlier research, now with ERGMs. Feedback-loop under-representation is not an independent functional finding once other topology is included. Catalog method is network motifs; stage graph analysis. Species in the abstract are E. coli and yeast for GRNs, plus an unnamed PPI network.

plain_language_summary: Biologists often ask whether a small wiring pattern appears more than chance would allow. This paper shows a statistical model that can test those patterns more carefully than older methods, using protein-interaction and gene-control networks as examples.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans offers both a connectome and whole-brain calcium imaging, a setting to relate synapse-level structure to network-level function.
ocar.challenge: Network-controllability analyses have used linear dynamics, and it is unclear whether real worm activity matches that assumption, or which control signals the network uses internally.
ocar.action: Fieseler, Zimmer, and Kutz fit a global low-dimensional model in which an underlying linear dynamical system is actuated by temporally sparse control signals, discovered in an unsupervised way from whole-brain recordings.
ocar.resolution: Discovered control signals are interpretable: they associate with transitions between expert-annotated behaviors, and they can be predicted from neurons previously implicated in those transitions plus additional neurons not previously associated. The framework can reveal transitions and encodings unsupervised and is described as generalizable to other neurosensory systems.
ocar.future_work: Generalization to other systems is proposed; the linear-plus-sparse-control form is still a model class, not a biophysical circuit diagram.

summaries.beginner: If you watch every cell in a worm brain, you can try to find the rare “steering” events that switch the animal from one action to another. This paper does that without using the usual behavior labels first, then shows that those events line up with known behavior changes and with particular cells.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of the Royal Society Interface (2020), Fieseler, Zimmer, and Kutz propose unsupervised learning of control signals from C. elegans whole-brain recordings. A global low-dimensional model treats activity as an underlying linear dynamical system actuated by temporally sparse controls. Those control signals associate with transitions between previously expert-annotated behaviors and can be predicted from neurons already implicated in such transitions as well as additional unassociated neurons. The authors contrast this with linear controllability analyses whose assumptions may not match real dynamics.
summaries.advanced: Interpretability is shown by post-hoc alignment to expert behavior labels and by decoding from identified neurons—not by proving the sparse inputs are the true synaptic controls. Additional predictive neurons are reported as previously unassociated; follow-up causal tests are not in the abstract. Catalog dataset DS01; stage infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: If you watch every cell in a worm brain, you can try to find the rare “steering” events that switch the animal from one action to another. This paper does that without using the usual behavior labels first, then shows that those events line up with known behavior changes and with particular cells.

ocar.opportunity: Macro/meso-scale connectomics (population-level) and micro-scale connectomics (neuron-to-neuron) have advanced separately; a whole-neocortex statistical micro-connectome would bridge them for simulation and as a null model.
ocar.challenge: No measured neuron-to-neuron map of an entire mouse neocortex exists, so a draft must be inferred from region-to-region data plus individual whole-brain axon reconstructions.
ocar.action: Reimann, Gevaert, Shi, Lu, Markram, and Muller combine meso-scale connectivity with whole-brain axon reconstructions to build a first-draft statistical model of the mouse whole-neocortex micro-connectome, revealing a targeting principle that predicts individual-axon innervation logic from meso-scale data.
ocar.resolution: The connectome recreates biological targeting trends on macro, meso, and micro scales and predicts that scale-invariant topological organization of connectivity extends down to individual neurons. It is offered as a powerful null model and as a substrate for whole-brain simulations.
ocar.future_work: This is a statistical draft, not a measured synapse-resolution neocortex; its value is as a null and simulation substrate to be tested against new reconstructions.

summaries.beginner: No one has measured every connection between neurons in an entire mouse cortex, but we do know how regions connect and how some single axons wander. This paper blends those ingredients into a statistical stand-in map that can be used as a baseline and for whole-brain simulations.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2019), Reimann, Gevaert, Shi, Lu, Markram, and Muller construct a first-draft statistical micro-connectome of the whole mouse neocortex from region-to-region connectivity and individual whole-brain axon reconstructions. A targeting principle predicts innervation logic of individual axons from meso-scale data. The resulting connectome recreates biological targeting trends at macro-, meso-, and micro-scales and predicts that an established principle of scale-invariant topological organization extends to individual neurons. The resource is framed as a null model and a substrate for whole-brain simulations.
summaries.advanced: “First draft statistical model” is the authors’ precise status: not an EM-complete neocortex. Scale-invariant topology extending to single neurons is a prediction of this model. Catalog stages graph analysis and modeling; organism mouse. Simulation usefulness depends on how well the targeting principle holds for unsampled axons.

plain_language_summary: No one has measured every connection between neurons in an entire mouse cortex, but we do know how regions connect and how some single axons wander. This paper blends those ingredients into a statistical stand-in map that can be used as a baseline and for whole-brain simulations.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian brains are networks of projections whose strengths vary widely; weights may add organization beyond binary topology.
ocar.challenge: Whether empirical weights specifically enhance clustering and rich-club integration, and whether that shows up in simulated dynamics, needs a high-resolution weighted connectome.
ocar.action: de Lange, Ardesch, and van den Heuvel perform weighted and binary network analyses on macaque cortico-cortical connectivity from the Markov et al. (2014) tract-tracing dataset, then simulate interactions with the Kuramoto model.
ocar.resolution: Both weighted and binary analyses show small-world, modular, and rich-club organization. Connection strength augments that architecture by enhancing local clustering and the central infrastructure for global communication. Kuramoto simulations show weights enhance synchronization within modules and between rich-club hubs.
ocar.future_work: Results are for this macaque tract-tracing matrix; other weighting schemes or incomplete sampling could change how much weights “augment” binary structure.

summaries.beginner: Brain regions are not only connected or not: some pathways are much stronger than others. In a monkey cortex map, this study finds that using those strengths, not just the yes/no skeleton, makes local groups tighter and the most central regions even more able to work together.
summaries.intermediate: In Network Neuroscience (2019), de Lange, Ardesch, and van den Heuvel analyze weighted versus binary versions of the macaque cortico-cortical connectome from Markov and colleagues (2014). Both versions show small-world, modular, and rich-club organization. Weights follow a distribution that augments the binary architecture by enhancing local clustering and the rich-club’s role in global communication and integration. Kuramoto model simulations indicate that connectivity-strength distribution enhances synchronization within modules and between rich-club hubs.
summaries.advanced: The Markov 2014 tract-tracing dataset is the sole empirical matrix; sampling and directionality conventions of that resource apply. “Augments” is relative to the binary version of the same graph. Kuramoto dynamics are a simulation, not recorded macaque physiology. Catalog organism is “other” (macaque); stages include proofreading, graph analysis, modeling.

plain_language_summary: Brain regions are not only connected or not: some pathways are much stronger than others. In a monkey cortex map, this study finds that using those strengths, not just the yes/no skeleton, makes local groups tighter and the most central regions even more able to work together.
